layout_dets.text: Abstract

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Machine Learning for Aerial Image Labeling

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Volodymyr Mnih

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Doctor of Philosophy

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Graduate Department of Computer Science

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: University of Toronto

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Information extracted from aerial photographs has found applications in a wide range

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of areas including urban planning, crop and forest management, disaster relief, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: climate modeling. At present, much of the extraction is still performed by human

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: experts, making the process slow, costly, and error prone. The goal of this thesis is to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: develop methods for automatically extracting the locations of objects such as roads,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: buildings, and trees directly from aerial images.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We investigate the use of machine learning methods trained on aligned aerial

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: images and possibly outdated maps for labeling the pixels of an aerial image with se-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mantic labels. We show how deep neural networks implemented on modern GPUs can

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be used to efficiently learn highly discriminative image features. We then introduce

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: new loss functions for training neural networks that are partially robust to incom-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: plete and poorly registered target maps. Finally, we propose two ways of improving

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the predictions of our system by introducing structure into the outputs of the neural

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: networks.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We evaluate our system on the largest and most-challenging road and building

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: detection datasets considered in the literature and show that it works reliably under

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a wide variety of conditions. Furthermore, we are releasing the first large-scale road

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and building detection datasets to the public in order to facilitate future comparisons

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with other methods.

layout_dets.text: Chapter 1

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Introduction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Aerial image interpretation is the process of examining aerial imagery for the purposes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of identifying objects and determining various properties of the identified objects. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: process originated during the First World War when photos taken from airplanes were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: examined for the purpose of reconnaissance. In its near one hundred year history,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aerial image interpretation has found applications in many diverse areas including

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: urban planning, crop and forest management, disaster relief, and climate modeling.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Much of the work, however, is still performed by human experts.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Examining large amounts of aerial imagery by hand is an expensive and time

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consuming process. First attempts at automation using computers date back to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the late 1960s and early 1970s [Idelsohn, 1970, Bajcsy and Tavakoli, 1976]. While

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: significant progress has been made in the past thirty years, only a few semi-automated

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: systems that work in limited domains are in use today and no fully automated systems

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: currently exist [Baltsavias, 2004, Mayer, 2008].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The recent explosion in the availability of high resolution imagery underscores

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the need for automated aerial image interpretation methods. Such imagery, having

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: resolution as high as 100 pixels per square meter, has greatly increased the number of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: possible applications but at the cost of an increase in the amount of required manual

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: processing. Recent applications of large-scale machine learning to such high-resolution

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: imagery have produced object detectors with impressive levels of accuracy [Kluckner

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and Bischof, 2009, Kluckner et al., 2009, Mnih and Hinton, 2010, 2012], suggesting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that automated aerial image interpretation systems may be within reach.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In machine learning applications, aerial image interpretation is usually formulated

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as a pixel labeling task. Given an aerial image like the one shown in Figure 1.1, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 1.1: An aerial image of the city of Boston.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: goal is to produce either a complete semantic segmentation of the image into classes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: such as building, road, tree, grass, and water [Kluckner and Bischof, 2009, Kluckner

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: et al., 2009] or a binary classification of the image for a single object class [Dollar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: et al., 2006, Mnih and Hinton, 2010, 2012].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: While image labeling or parsing of general scenes has been extensively studied [He

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: et al., 2004, Shotton et al., 2008, Farabet et al., 2012], aerial images have a few distinct

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: characteristics that make aerial image labeling an easier task. First, by restricting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ourselves to overhead imagery with known ground resolution both the viewpoint

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and the scale of objects can be assumed to be fixed. Having a fixed viewpoint and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: scale reduces the possible variations in object appearance and makes the priors on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: object shape less broad than in general image labeling. This suggests that it should

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be possible to incorporate strong shape dependencies into an aerial image labeling

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: systems. Finally, the amount of both unlabeled and labeled aerial imagery is massive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: compared to the datasets available for general image labeling tasks. Methods that are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: able to effectively learn from massive amounts of labeled data should have a distinct

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: advantage on aerial image labeling tasks over methods that can't.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The goal of this thesis is to develop new machine learning methods that are par-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ticularly well suited to the task of aerial image labeling. Namely, this thesis focuses

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on what we see as the three main issues in applying image labeling techniques to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aerial imagery:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: • Context and Features: The use of context is important for successfully label-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ing aerial images because local colour cues are not sufficient for discriminating

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between pairs of object classes like trees and grass, and roads and buildings

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Additionally, occlusions and shadows caused by trees and tall buildings often

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: make it impossible to classify a pixel without using any context information.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Since the number of input features grows quadratically with the width of an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: input image patch, the number of parameters and the amount of computation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: required for a naive approach also increases quadratically. For these reasons,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: efficient ways of extracting discriminative features from a large image context

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are necessary for aerial image labeling.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: • Noisy Labels: When training a system to label images, the amount of labeled

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: training data tends to be a limiting factor. The most successful applications of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: machine learning to aerial imagery have relied on existing maps. These provide

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abundant labels, but the labels are often incomplete and sometimes poorly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: registered, which hurts the performance of object detectors trained on them. In

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: order to successfully apply image labeling to buildings and other object types

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for which the amount of label noise is high, new learning methods that are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: robust to noise in the labels are required.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: • Structured Outputs: Labels of nearby pixels in an image exhibit strong

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: correlations, and exploiting this structure can significantly improve labeling

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accuracy. Due to the restricted viewpoint and fixed scale of aerial imagery,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the structure present in the labels is generally more rigid than that in general

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: image labeling, with shape playing an important role. In addition to being able

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to handle shape constraints, a structured prediction method suited to aerial

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: imagery should also be able to deal with large datasets and noisy labels.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The main contribution of this thesis is a coherent framework for learning to label

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aerial imagery. The proposed framework consists of a patch-based formulation of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aerial image labeling, new deep neural network architectures implemented on GPUs,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and new loss functions for training these architectures, resulting in a single model

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that can be trained end-to-end while dealing with the issues of context, noisy labels,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and structured outputs.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Fully embracing the view of aerial image labeling as a large scale machine learning

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: task, we assemble a number of road and building detection datasets that far surpass

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: all previous work in terms of both size and difficulty. In addition to releasing the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: first publicly available datasets for aerial image labeling we perform the first truly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: large-scale evaluation of an aerial image labeling system on real-world data. When

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: trained on these road and building detection datasets our models surpass all published

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: models in terms of accuracy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The rest of the thesis is organized as follows:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: • Chapter 2 presents a brief overview of existing work on applying machine learn-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ing to aerial image data. Some related work on general image labeling that has

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not been applied to aerial imagery is also covered.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: • Chapter 3 presents our formulation of aerial image labeling as a patch-based

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pixel labeling task as well as an evaluation of several different proposed architec-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tures. The main contribution is a GPU-based, deep convolutional architecture

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that is capable of exploiting a large image context as well as learning discrim-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inative features. This chapter includes work previously published in Mnih and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Hinton [2010] and Mnih and Hinton [2012].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: • Chapter 4 addresses the problem of learning from incomplete or poorly regis-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tered maps. The main contributions are loss functions that provide robustness

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to both types of label noise and are suitable for training the architectures pro-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: posed in Chapter 3. This work has been previously published in [Mnih and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Hinton, 2012].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: • Chapter 5 explores ways of taking advantage of the structure present in the la-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bels. We investigate two complementary ways of performing structured predic-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion – post-processing neural networks and Conditional Random Fields (CRFs).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We argue that neural networks are good at learning high-level structure while

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CRFs are good at capturing low-level dependencies, with the combination of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the two approaches being particularly effective. We also show how to combine

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a noise model from Chapter 4 with the proposed structured prediction models.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: This chapter includes work previously published in Mnih et al. [2011] and Mnih

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and Hinton [2012].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: • Chapter 6 introduces the first large-scale publicly available datasets for road

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and building detection which are both much larger and more challenging than

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: any datasets previously used in the literature. We evaluate our most promis-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ing models on the new datasets giving an indication of how well the proposed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: algorithms work in the wild.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: • Chapter 7 summarizes our most important findings and offers a discussion of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the most promising directions for improving our system.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Chapter 2

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: An Overview of Aerial Image

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Labeling

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: This chapter aims to present a general overview of aerial image labeling methods. In

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: particular, we focus on approaches that make use of machine learning as opposed to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ad-hoc and knowledge-based approaches [Idelsohn, 1970, Bajcsy and Tavakoli, 1976,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Kettig and Landgrebe, 1976, Jr. et al., 1985] which account for much of the early

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: work on automating aerial image interpretation. While knowledge-based approaches

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have led to some operational systems in limited domains, machine learning has led

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to much of the recent progress in aerial image interpretation as well as progress on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: related computer vision problems such as semantic image labeling [Shotton et al.,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We will use the term aerial imagery to refer to any type of two dimensional and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: possibly multi-band data collected by an airborne sensor. In addition to imagery

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: taken by sensors that measure visible light, this includes sensors that measure other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: kinds of electromagnetic radiation, such as infrared and hyperspectral sensors, as well

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as sensors that do not measure electromagnetic radiation, such as airborne LIDAR,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which measures the distance to objects from the sensor.

layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 2. AN OVERVIEW OF AERIAL IMAGE LABELING

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2.1 Early Work - Simple Classifiers and Local Fea-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tures

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Some of the first applications of machine learning to aerial imagery considered the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: task of classifying land cover, or terrain, into different classes, such as forest, water,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: agricultural land, and built-up land. Early approaches tried to predict the discrete

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: class label

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at a pixel i from a vector

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of features at i [Decatur, 1989, Benediktsson

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: et al., 1990, Bischof et al., 1993, Paola and Schowengerdt, 1995], with the features

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: typically just taken to be the values at the different spectral bands at pixel i.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The Bayes' classifier is one of simplest and most popular approaches to terrain

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: classification. The Bayes' classifier makes explicit assumptions about the class condi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tional distributions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and the prior class probabilities

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and uses

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bayes' rule to obtain the posterior class probabilities

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: . Typically, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: class conditional distribution

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is assumed to have a multivariate normal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distribution with mean

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and covariance

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: . Various simplifying assumptions lead

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to other popular classifiers. For example, assuming that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is diagonal leads to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Naive Bayes classifier for continuous inputs while assuming that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: leads to what is known in the remote sensing literature as the maximum likelihood

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: classifier [Paola and Schowengerdt, 1995].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The main drawback of the Bayes' classifier is the need to explicitly specify the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: class-conditional distribution

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: . Since the multivariate normal distribu-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion is typically used for the class-conditional distributions, only linear or quadratic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: decision boundaries can be learned by such a model. Neural networks became a pop-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ular alternative to the Bayes' classifier because they directly model

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: differentiable function whose parameters are learned [Decatur, 1989, Lee et al., 1990,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bischof et al., 1993]. This both sidesteps the need to specify

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: , and allows

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for richer, non-linear decision boundaries to be learned when at least one hidden layer

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of units with a non-linear activation function is used. Due to the ability to learn non-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: linear decision boundaries neural networks tend to give higher classification accuracies

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: than various forms of the Bayes' classifier [Decatur, 1989, Benediktsson et al., 1990].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bischof et al. [Bischof et al., 1993] and Boggess [Boggess, 1993] explored adding

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contextual information by using spectral values from a small patch centered at the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pixel of interest as the input to a neural network, allowing it to learn some contex-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tual features. However, such features were still very local since they used at most

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 2. AN OVERVIEW OF AERIAL IMAGE LABELING

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a 7 by 7 window for context. Others aimed to improve classification accuracy by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: using hand-designed features that encode local textural information [Haralick et al.,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1973, Haralick, 1976, Lee et al., 1990]. Haralick et al. [Haralick, 1976] introduced

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a popular set of features derived from gray level spatial dependence matrices

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: where

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: specifies the frequency at which gray level values i and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: co-occur

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at distance d and angle θ. Statistical quantities derived from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: were shown to be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: good for discriminating between different types of textures. For example, the sum of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: squares of the entries of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: can be used to discriminate coarse textures from fine

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: textures because the sum of squares should be higher for coarse textures than for fine

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: textures when d is small.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Since such systems were generally applied to low resolution imagery, with a single

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pixel representing as much as 30x30 meters, local spectral cues were sufficient for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: discriminating between broad classes of interest, such as forest and farmland, with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reasonably high accuracy. For example Bischof et al. [Bischof et al., 1993] report

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accuracies in the range of 85% on a four class classification task using only the values

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of seven spectral bands as input.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: However, with increasing availability of higher resolution data, the focus shifted

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to classifying aerial imagery into finer object classes, such as roads, cars, and trees.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: At resolutions higher than one pixel per square meter, differences in object type,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shape and material as well as variations in weather and lighting conditions make it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: impossible to accurately classify objects based on local cues alone.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2.2 Move to High-Resolution Data

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The Ikonos and Quickbird satellites, launched in 1999 and 2001 respectively, began

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: acquiring panchromatic images of the surface of the Earth at resolutions of roughly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one square meter per pixel, significantly increasing the number of possible applications

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of aerial image interpretation systems. Since at this resolution the classes of interest

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are man-made objects such as buildings, roads, and cars, the approach of training

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: simple classifiers on very local spectral and textural features that was moderately

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: successful on low resolution images no longer leads to acceptable accuracy levels.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The approaches discussed in the previous section no longer work because they were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generally designed to do local texture classification, but the problem of classifying

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: high-resolution imagery is much more complex, requiring knowledge of shape and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 2. AN OVERVIEW OF AERIAL IMAGE LABELING

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: context in addition to texture.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: During the move from low-resolution to high-resolution image labeling the most

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: notable trends were:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1. The switch to more powerful or sophisticated classifiers such as AdaBoost,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: SVMs, and random forests.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2. The use of more spatial context and richer input features.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3. The use of much more data for training and testing.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 4. The use of structured prediction methods such as Conditional Random Fields.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We will discuss the first three trends in some detail in the following subsections and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: delay the discussion of structured prediction methods to a later, separate section.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2.2.1 Better classifiers

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Discriminating between object classes with similar texture, such as roads and build-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ings, requires some knowledge of shape and context, which in turn leads to much

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more complex decision boundaries than the ones required for discriminating between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: wooded and built up areas in low-resolution imagery. Due to the need to learn such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: highly nonlinear decision boundaries, applications of machine learning to high reso-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lution imagery have relied on more sophisticated classifiers such as SVMs, random

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: forests and various types of boosting.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: While neural networks are able to learn nonlinear decision boundaries and have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: been widely used in remote sensing applications, many researchers found them difficult

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to train due to the presence of local optima [Benediktsson et al., 1990]. Support Vector

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Machines presented an attractive alternative to neural networks because, like neural

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: networks, they are able to learn nonlinear decision boundaries, but, unlike neural

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: networks, SVMs optimize a convex loss function and do not suffer from the problem

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of local optima. Since SVMs are essentially sophisticated template matchers and have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: been shown to work poorly when applied as classifiers to raw image patches [LeCun

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: et al., 2004], they are generally used in combination with higher level features in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the computer vision community [Lazebnik et al., 2006]. Applications of SVMs to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aerial image interpretation have been much more primitive than in the computer

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 2. AN OVERVIEW OF AERIAL IMAGE LABELING

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vision community, with most papers using SVMs to classify pixels using only low-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: level features [Huang et al., 2002, Song et al., 2005].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Some of the more successful approaches to labeling high resolution aerial imagery

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have relied on various ensemble methods, with boosting and random forests being

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: particularly popular. Porway et al. [2008] developed a hierarchical model for aerial

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: image parsing that relied on bottom up detectors for cars, roads, parking lots and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: buildings that were trained using different types of boosting. Other notable applica-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tions of boosting include the work of Dollar et al. [Dollar et al., 2006], who developed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a general framework for learning to detect image boundaries using a boosted pixel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: classifier and presented some qualitative results on road detection, and the work of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Nguyen et al. [Nguyen et al., 2007] who used online boosting to learn a car detector.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A common reason for using boosting in these applications is its ability to perform

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: feature selection from a very large pool of features when the set of weak learners is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: restricted to learners that look at a single feature. Dollar et al. [2006] were able to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: use a pool of 50,000 filter responses as features for their edge classifier.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A random forest is another tree-based ensemble method that has been widely

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: used in image labeling applications. A random forest classifier consists of a number

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of decision trees whose predictions are typically combined using majority voting. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: goal of the training procedure is to reduce the variance of the ensemble by trying to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: produce decorrelated trees. This is achieved by learning each tree on a random subset

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the dataset and using a random subset of the input variables. A number of papers

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by Kluckner et al. [Kluckner et al., 2009, Kluckner and Bischof, 2009] use random

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: forests for performing semantic classification of aerial images with impressive results.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: While random forests and boosting of tree classifiers both construct ensembles of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: trees, they do so in completely different ways, leading to clear advantages and dis-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: advantages that may make one more suitable to aerial imagery applications. While

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: boosting has been found to perform better than random forests in several bake offs,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: algorithms such as AdaBoost are known to perform poorly in the presence of outliers

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or mislabeled training cases because they tend to emphasize the difficult cases during

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: training. This may be a serious limitation in the context of aerial image interpreta-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion because perfectly registered and up-to-date label information is rarely available.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Random forests, on the other hand, are much less affected by mislabeled data because

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: each tree is built on a random subset of the training data using a random subset of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the input features and no special emphasis is placed on the difficult training cases.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 2. AN OVERVIEW OF AERIAL IMAGE LABELING

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Additionally, random forests are embarrassingly parallelizable while boosting is much

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more difficult to parallelize due to its sequential nature. Given these reasons random

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: forests seem to be somewhat better suited to aerial image classification.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2.2.2 Better features

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The approach of using the values of multiple bands at a single pixel, or even a window

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of a small size such as 5x5, as input to a classifier is hopeless on high resolution

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: imagery because the input simply does not contain enough information to discriminate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between object classes. The simplest way of addressing this problem is to use a larger

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: input window as input. Mnih and Hinton [Mnih and Hinton, 2010] showed that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: increasing the size of the input patch from 24 by 24, which is already a large context

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: size compared to other work, to 64 by 64 significantly improves precision and recall

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on a road detection task.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Simply using a large image patch for input can be slow even on modern computers

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: because the computational cost of applying a linear filter to a square patch scales

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: quadratically with the width of the patch. For this reason recent work has relied on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: efficiently computable features in order to scale up to large context sizes [Kluckner

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and Bischof, 2009, Nguyen et al., 2007, Dollar et al., 2006]. The most widely used class

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of efficiently computable image features is the set of features that can be expressed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as a linear combination of sums of rectangular regions of the image [Viola and Jones,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2001]. To compute such filters efficiently, let

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be the value of the image intensity

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of a single channel at location

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and define

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: S is known as the integral image of I and can be computed in time linear in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: number of pixels in the image. Once S is computed, the sum of any sub-rectangle of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: I can be computed in constant time. For example, the sum of I over the rectangle

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: can be computed as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: . Features that can

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be computed efficiently using the integral image trick include special cases of Haar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: wavelets [Viola and Jones, 2001] and histograms of oriented gradients.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Typically, people rely on filters from one or more popular filter banks for obtaining

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: input representations. Filters in the Haar basis, shown in Figure 3.10 (top), consist

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 2. AN OVERVIEW OF AERIAL IMAGE LABELING

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 2.1: Filters from widely used filter banks. Top) Haar. Middle) Oriented

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Gaussian derivatives. Bottom) Oriented Gabors.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of axis aligned rectangles and produce the largest outputs when strong edges in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: image align with the edges in the filter. In order to detect non-axis aligned edges more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: easily, filters based on oriented derivatives of Gaussians have been used. The popular

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: filter bank proposed by Leung and Malik uses oriented first and second derivatives

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of a Gaussian at three scales and six orientations, shown in Figure 3.10 (middle).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Filters based on oriented Gabor wavelets, shown in Figure 3.10 (bottom), are good

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at detecting parallel oriented edges and are commonly used for exploiting textural

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: information. Since computing a large number of such features for each image patch

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: can be expensive, either a small number of filters tend to be used, such as in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Leung and Malik filter bank, or a feature selection approach, such as boosting, is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: used to select a few of the filters from a large pool of candidate filters. Dollar et al.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [2006] replicated a filter bank similar to the one pictured in Figure 3.10 over multiple

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: locations of a 50x50 patch for a total of over 50000 filters and used boosting to select

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a small subset of them. When no feature selection is performed, specialized hardware,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: such as GPUs, can be used for learning with a large number of features [Mnih and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Hinton, 2010] because such hardware tends to be much faster than modern CPUs at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: performing dense linear algebra operations.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A more recent trend in aerial image labeling is the use of unsupervised feature

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: learning methods such as sparse coding and Restricted Boltzmann Machines [Mnih

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and Hinton, 2010]. Using features learned by a Restricted Boltzmann Machine to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: initialize a neural network trained on a road detection task has been shown to signifi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cantly improve both precision and recall over training a neural network from random

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: initialization [Mnih and Hinton, 2010]. Rigamonti et al. [2011] used a variant of sparse

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: coding to learn features for several linear structure segmentation tasks. While their

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: qualitative results on road detection are not very good, their system obtains state-of-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 2. AN OVERVIEW OF AERIAL IMAGE LABELING

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the-art performance on a retinal blood vessel segmentation task. Such unsupervised

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: feature learning approaches tend to learn filters that resemble oriented edge detectors

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and Gabor wavelets [Mnih and Hinton, 2010, Rigamonti et al., 2011] and have the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: advantage of potentially being able to learn the best filters for the task at hand as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposed to just selecting the best ones from a pool of features that appear at only a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: few scales and orientations.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A different type of feature that has been shown to be immensely useful for aerial

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: image interpretation is height information. Kluckner et al. [Kluckner et al., 2009]

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: showed that using height in addition to rich appearance-only features boosts classifi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cation accuracies by 10 to 20%. The result should not be surprising because height

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: information can help discriminate between very confusable pairs of objects such as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: roads/buildings and grass/trees. Height information can either be derived directly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from LIDAR data or from overlapping image pairs using stereo techniques. While

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: extremely helpful, height information may be difficult to obtain because LIDAR data

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is less widely available and more expensive than aerial imagery, and most aerial im-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: agery comes in the form of non-overlapping orthorectified image tiles which do not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contain stereo information.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2.2.3 Larger datasets

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In early work on aerial image labeling it was common to use a single image for both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: training and testing [Bischof et al., 1993, Bruzzone and Prieto, 2000]. Such a small

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: amount of data cannot possibly cover a large range of variations in the appearance

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of various objects leading to classifiers that are unlikely to work well on unseen data.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The limited size of the test set as well as its similarity to the training data means

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that the accuracy levels reported in earlier work are unlikely to translate to larger

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: datasets. Recent applications of machine learning to high-resolution aerial imagery

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have used much more training data. For example, Porway et al. [2008] used 120 images

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ranging in size from 640x480 to 1000x1000 for training their hierarchical probabilistic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammar model of aerial image annotations. Kluckner et al. [Kluckner et al., 2009,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Kluckner and Bischof, 2009] used three datasets of roughly 100 images with each

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dataset covering between 5 and 8 square kilometers to train a random forest classifier,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: while Mnih and Hinton [Mnih and Hinton, 2010] trained a large neural network on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 130 large images that cover an area of roughly 500 square kilometers at a resolution of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 2. AN OVERVIEW OF AERIAL IMAGE LABELING

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 0.7 pixels per square meter. Datasets of this size are more likely to contain significant

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: variations in the appearance of objects and, when used for training, these datasets

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: make it much harder for powerful classifiers to overfit.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2.3 Structured Prediction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The labels of nearby image pixels tend to be highly dependent due to the spatial

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: coherence of images and incorporating such knowledge into a predictor should improve

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: its accuracy. This idea of exploiting structure in the output labels was used in some of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the earliest work on aerial image labeling [Kettig and Landgrebe, 1976] and continues

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to be important. This section provides an overview of the three main approaches

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to structured prediction, namely segmentation, post-classification, and probabilistic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: approaches.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2.3.1 Segmentation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Segmentation-based approaches work by first segmenting an image and then classify-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ing entire regions instead of individual pixels. Such approaches were among the first

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to be proposed and are still in use today, usually in combination with a probabilistic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: approach. In early work, Kettig and Landgrebe [Kettig and Landgrebe, 1976] pro-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: posed a procedure that first classified non-overlapping aerial image patches of size

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 4 by 4 into homogeneous and non-homogeneous regions. The non-homogeneous re-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: gions were then classified pixel-by-pixel, while homogeneous regions were merged into

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: larger regions and then classified using a region classifier. The standard approach is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to oversegment the image into what are known as superpixels and then classify the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: superpixels individually [He et al., 2006, Huang and Zhang, 2009]. A statistical ap-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proach such as a Conditional Random Field can then be used to exploit dependencies

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in neighbouring superpixel labels, as was done by He at al. [He et al., 2006].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: While initially used as a structured prediction method, more recently segmentation-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: based methods have been used for reducing the complexity of image labeling prob-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lems [He et al., 2006]. Labeling a few hundred superpixels per image can be a lot

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: less computationally demanding than labeling thousands of pixels, allowing for more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complex models to be used. The main drawback of segmentation-based approaches

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to structured prediction is that they are usually unable to recover from incorrect seg-

layout_dets.label: display_formula
layout_dets.latex: P ( \mathbf { y } | \mathbf { x } ) = \exp \left( - \sum _ { c \in C } f _ { c } ( \mathbf { y } _ { c } , \mathbf { x } ) \right) / Z ( \mathbf { x } ) ,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 2. AN OVERVIEW OF AERIAL IMAGE LABELING

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mentations, which can be particularly problematic in the aerial image setting where

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: occlusion of objects by trees or buildings is common. Some extensions of this approach

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: can reduce such failures by generating multiple oversegmentations using different pa-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rameter settings and combining classifications of the different segmentations into a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: single classification of the pixels [Kohli et al., 2009].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2.3.2 Post-classification

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Post-classification approaches aim to let predictions at one pixel indirectly influence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predictions at nearby pixels. For example, salt and pepper noise can be reduced

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: without any learning by applying a majority vote filter to the outputs of a local

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: classifier. Alternatively, some classifier is used to obtain preliminary labels for all the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pixels and a second classifier is then trained to predict a new label for each pixel based

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on the preliminary labels of nearby pixels. The hope is that this second classifier will

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be able to clean up the output of the first classifier. Bischof et al. [Bischof et al.,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1993] trained a neural network that looks at a 5x5 window of predictions to predict a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: new label for the middle pixel, improving classification accuracy by several percent.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Mnih and Hinton [Mnih and Hinton, 2010] used a neural network with a 64x64 input

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: window to clean up predictions of another neural network on a road detection task,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: significantly improving both precision and recall

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2.3.3 Probabilistic Approaches

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Probabilistic approaches directly model the conditional probability

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the la-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bels y given the image x. By far the most widely used probabilistic model for struc-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tured prediction is the conditional random field, which models

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as a Markov

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: random field over the labels y that is globally-conditioned on the image x. More

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: precisely

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: where C is a set of cliques over y,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are potential functions, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is the partition

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: function.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The most widely used form of CRFs in both aerial imaging applications and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the field of computer vision in general is the pairwise CRF, for which the model

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: model has two types of potentials.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is the unary potential which determines how

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: well label

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: agrees with the image x, while

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is an interaction potential which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: determines how well the labels at sites i and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: agree with each other and, possibly,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the image x.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In image labeling applications of CRFs the graphical structure of the model is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: almost always either a lattice or a tree. In a typical lattice the sites are laid out on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a grid with each site connected to either its 4 or 8 neighbours, depending on whether

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the diagonal neighbours are connected. The lattice structure is generally used when

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the pixels themselves or rectangular sets of pixels are used as the labeling sites. Such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CRFs have been applied to urban area detection [Zhong and Wang, 2007] and LIDAR

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: point classification [Niemeyer et al., 2008]. Tree structured CRFs are typically used

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: when the labeling sites are regions obtained by first segmenting the image. This

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: technique is often used for significantly reducing the number of random variables

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: over which the CRF is defined in order to speed up inference and learning [Modestino

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and Zhang, 1989].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Pairwise CRFs are appealing for their simplicity, but since they use only pairwise

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: interaction potentials they seem to restrict one to only being able to encourage label

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: smoothness constraints. While smoothness is probably the most important constraint

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for aerial image labeling applications, being able to include other types of constraints

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is desirable. For example, the fact that roads tend to have different shape than

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: buildings is a very strong cue for distinguishing between roads and buildings. In

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: order to incorporate such knowledge into a model one would need to be able to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: encode constraints on shape. Similarly, constraints based on layout could be useful

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for detecting buildings because buildings tend to be next to roads. The multiscale

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CRF model proposed by He et al. [2004] is an alternative to pairwise CRFs that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is able to learn the shape and layout of objects. For the case of binary labels y,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the CRF of He et al. [2004] is a conditional Restricted Boltzmann Machine with the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and the model parameters are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corresponds to a single feature of the labels y and can encode possible

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shapes of objects as well as different arrangements of objects.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Probabilistic approaches to structured prediction are the most principled since

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: they can directly enforce smoothness and other constraints on the labels. The ability

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to model complex distributions, however, often makes exact or efficient inference

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: intractable. In the case of CRFs, the models for which exact inference is tractable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tend to be simple models such as tree-structured CRFs, or lattice-structured CRFs

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with sub-modular potentials. When working with more expressive classes of CRFs

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one generally has to resort to approximate inference and learning procedures, making

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the application of such models difficult.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2.3.4 Discussion of Structured Prediction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Out of the approaches to structured prediction we have discussed, methods based

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on segmentation are the weakest because of their rigidity. Due to this weakness,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: segmentation-based methods are now rarely used without being combined with a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: probabilistic model. Nevertheless, segmentations of an image can provide useful

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contextual information and have been used to construct new high-level image fea-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tures [Shotton et al., 2008] for use in CRFs. Post-classification approaches can work

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: well when a large training set is available [Mnih and Hinton, 2010], but such meth-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ods only incorporate indirect dependencies between the labels through the cleanup

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: process and are not as principled as probabilistic approaches. The combination of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: post-classification approach with a probabilistic model, such as a CRF, offers an inter-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: esting possibility. Since incorporating rich dependencies among the labels y generally

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: leads to intractable inference, applying a CRF in which exact inference is tractable to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the outputs of a classifier would allow for incorporating complex dependencies over

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the outputs without having to resort to inefficient or approximate inference.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 2. AN OVERVIEW OF AERIAL IMAGE LABELING

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2.4 Source of Supervision

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: One important, yet rarely discussed, aspect of using machine learning for aerial im-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: age interpretation is the source of the data. The vast majority of papers rely on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hand-labeled data for both training and testing [Bischof et al., 1993, Nguyen et al.,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2007, Porway et al., 2008, Kluckner et al., 2009, Kluckner and Bischof, 2009, Nguyen

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: et al., 2010] and since labeling images is a very time consuming process, the datasets

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have been small in both aerial image applications and general image labeling work.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A typical aerial image dataset covers a relatively small area of a single city, ranging

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anywhere between one square kilometer and ten square kilometers [Kluckner et al.,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2009, Kluckner and Bischof, 2009], which seriously limits the variability due to archi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tectural styles, weather conditions, and seasonal variations. Good results obtained

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by training and testing an image labeling approach on such a small amount of data

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: will not necessarily translate to good performance on an entire city, especially if the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: city is different from the one seen during training. Hence, obtaining good sources

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of accurately labeled data is important for both evaluating existing approaches and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: training systems that are likely to work under varying conditions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In some domains hand-labeling data in order to train a classifier is not necessary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: because the label information is often readily available. For example, in the case

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of road detection the locations of existing roads are typically known because they

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are useful for navigation and not just as target labels in a machine learning task.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The abundance of accurately labeled data for road detection makes it a very good

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: candidate for evaluating existing aerial image interpretation systems as well as the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: application of machine learning techniques. While recent work on road detection

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: has largely switched to using large, freely-available sources of data, such as Google

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Maps [Dollar et al., 2006, Huang and Zhang, 2009, Rigamonti et al., 2011], these

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: papers still do not use very much data for training and testing.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: For buildings, Google Maps can provide the locations of a substantial portion of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the buildings in almost any major city. This type of data can act as a source of noisy

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: labels, which are correct with very high probability when they indicate the presence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of an object and with lower, but still high, probability when they indicate the absence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of an object. Training a classifier on large amounts of this type of noisy data with a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: robust loss function can potentially produce a much better detector than by using a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: much smaller set of accurate labels. At present, there seem to be no applications of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 2. AN OVERVIEW OF AERIAL IMAGE LABELING

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: robust estimators to aerial image data with noisy labels.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: For object classes such as cars or areas for which Google Maps possesses neither

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accurate nor complete map information, hand-labeling data seems to be the only

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: option. While the use of crowdsourcing tools like Amazon Mechanical Turk can make

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it easier to collect label information, the process can still be expensive and time

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consuming to set up. When only a limited amount of labeled data is available it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is often possible to generate new labeled data by transforming existing data. In a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: classification task, small translations or rotations can be applied to the input images,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: but in order to apply the same idea to image labeling one must be able to realistically

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transform both the image and the labels. On a road detection task, applying rotations

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to each training case before it is processed has been shown to help prevent overfitting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and drastically improve performance on cities not seen during training [Mnih and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Hinton, 2010]. Applying affine photometric transformations to training images has

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: been shown to improve performance in a general image labeling task [Shotton et al.,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2008], and can be potentially even more useful for aerial imagery, where this process

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: could simulate things like varying levels of sunlight.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Chapter 3

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Learning to Label Aerial Images

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: This chapter presents our patch-based framework for learning to label aerial images

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and is divided into three parts. The first part describes the general framework, how

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: we use neural networks within the framework, as well as issues relating to generating

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: data and training and evaluating the models. In the second part of the chapter we

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: attempt to answer the question of what is a good neural network architecture for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aerial image labeling tasks by performing an extensive experimental comparison of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: different architectures. In the last part, we present a qualitative evaluation of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: best neural network architecture on road and building detection tasks and attempt

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to shed some light on what the neural networks are actually learning.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3.1 Patch-Based Labeling Framework

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The input to our aerial image labeling system is a list of aerial images

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and a list of corresponding map images

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: . The aerial images

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are assumed to be rectangular images with c channels and can be anything from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: gray scale

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: RGB aerial images to elevation maps and hyperspectral images. For

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: each

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the map or label image

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: denoting the label for the ith pixel of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: . For binary image labeling tasks,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: will be either 1 or 0, typically representing the presence or absence of an object of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: some class of interest. For multi-class problems,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: will take on values from a set

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of possible labels

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: . Figure 3.1 shows an example of an aerial image on the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: For now we will ignore the dependencies among nearby labels and assume conditional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: we consider the problem of dealing with noisy labels in Chapter 4.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We propose modeling the observed map distribution using neural networks. Neu-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ral networks are particularly well suited to aerial image labeling tasks because of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: several distinct advantages. Most importantly, neural networks have been shown to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: work particularly well on perceptual tasks with large amounts of labeled data, out-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: performing expert-designed systems in multiple domains [Dahl et al., 2010, Sermanet

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: et al., 2012]. The large amounts of existing maps suggests that this success could

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: apply to tasks such as road and building detection, for which large labeled training

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sets can be constructed. Another important benefit is the ease with which neural net-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: works can be parallelized on modern GPUs, which will make it possible to efficiently

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: scale up our models to large input contexts and train them on large datasets.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We will use f to denote the functional form of our neural network model, which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: maps an input aerial patch s to a distribution over the label patch m.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: will always

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have one input for each entry of s, but the number of outputs is determined by the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: number of possible labels.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: For binary labeling tasks, we use neural networks that have one output unit for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: each pixel of the map patch m with the output of unit i representing the predicted

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: probability that the ith label is 1. Since they encode probabilities, these output units

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3.1.1 Learning

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We learn the parameters of the neural networks by minimizing the negative log like-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lihood of the training data under our model. For binary data, the negative log

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: likelihood under the model in Equation 3.2 takes the form of a cross entropy between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the map patch m and the predicted label probabilities

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The outer sum of the objective

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is over all possible patches in the training data.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Since there is a very large number of patches in our dataset we use stochastic gradient

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: descent with minibatches for optimizing L. For datasets that fit in memory, we

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generate minibatches by repeatedly selecting a random pair

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and sampling

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a random patch from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: . For datasets that don't fit in memory, we keep

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a buffer of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pairs of image/label images in memory and generate minibatches by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sampling patches at random from this buffer. By periodically replacing one of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pairs in the buffer with one of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pairs outside the buffer we approximate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: random sampling of patches from the entire dataset.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Preprocessing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We have not explored the issue of preprocessing with the exception of relatively simple

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contrast normalization. We normalize each input patch by subtracting the average

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: value computed over the patch and dividing by the standard deviation computed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: over the entire dataset. Using more sophisticated types of preprocessing, such a local

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contrast normalization is likely to lead to additional improvements in performance.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Adding Rotations

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We found that it is useful to rotate each pair of image and label patches by a random

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: angle during learning. Since many cities have large areas where the road network

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: forms a grid, training on data without rotations will result in a model that is better at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: detecting roads and buildings at certain orientations. Figure 3.3 shows three patches

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: taken from the Toronto Roads dataset with a clear bias in the orientations of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: roads. By randomly rotating the training cases the resulting models do not favour

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: objects in any particular orientation. The improvement is particularly noticeable on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: infrequently appearing objects like highways, for which the orientation bias can be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: even stronger than for normal roads.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Tuning Hyperparameters

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: When training neural nets with stochastic gradient descent one generally has to set a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: number of hyper parameters including the learning rate, the amount of momentum

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the type and amount of weight decay, the mini batch size, and possibly others. We

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: did not separately tune these parameters for each architecture because doing so would

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: require a massive amount of computation. We chose the values of hyperparameters

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shared by all models by selecting the values that maximize the performance of a shal-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: low fully-connected network on the validation set of the Toronto Roads dataset. In

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the few cases where we tried tuning the values of these hyperparameters for individ-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ual models or architectures we saw slight improvements in precision and recall, but

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the order of models in terms of performance remained the same as for fixed hyperpa-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rameters. For this reason we believe that using the same values for hyperparameters

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shared by all models is a reasonable thing to do when comparing models. Table 3.1

layout_dets.text: shows the hyperparameter values used for the comparisons in this chapter.
