layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3.1.2 Generating Labels

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In order to train our labeling system, we need an abundant source of aerial images

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with pixel-level labels. While high-resolution imagery of many parts of the world

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is easy to obtain, per-pixel labels are scarce because they are mostly of interest as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: labels in a machine learning task. Hence per-pixel labels must be derived from other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: types of data. As we discussed in Chapter 2 the locations of many roads, buildings,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and other objects are freely available through the OpenStreetMap project in vector

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: format. While this data is often incomplete and noisy, it is still the largest freely

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: available source of such information which can be used to construct approximate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: per-pixel labels for training our systems.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We must decide on a way of converting vector maps to pixel-level labels before

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: we can use vector maps to train a pixel labeling system. The way vector labels are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rasterized will clearly have some effect on how well a system learns to label images,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: but in order to evaluate how good the rasterization procedure is one needs access

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to accurate per-pixel labels. Since we do not have access to such data we resort to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: using rasterized labels for both training and evaluation purposes. This means that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: our rasterization procedure ends up as a somewhat arbitrary choice and there are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: likely other, better ways of converting vector labels to pixel-labels. Nevertheless, by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: visualizing the predictions of different models trained with our rasterization procedure

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: we found that large differences in our evaluation metrics correspond to noticeable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: visual qualitative differences in the predictions and that the best systems indeed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: produce very good quality predictions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We now describe our rasterization procedure. Vector maps consist of three types

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of objects: polygons, lines, and points. Polygons are generally used to provide rea-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sonably accurate outlines of parks and building footprints, and hence they can simply

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be rasterized to obtain a per-pixel label map M. Some care must be taken with lines

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which tend to represent structures like roads and rivers, and points, which tend to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 3. LEARNING TO LABEL AERIAL IMAGES

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: represent small objects like houses and trees, because the vector representations do

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not provide per-pixel information. We attempt to generate reasonable soft per-pixel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: labels by applying simple smoothing to the rasterized objects. We define the label

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: map

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for linear or point features as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: where

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is the Euclidean distance, in pixels, between location i and the nearest

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: object in the map. The smoothing parameter σ depends on the scale of the aerial

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: images being used as well as the type of object being rasterized. For example

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: should

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: probably be higher for roads than for trees. This soft weighting scheme accounts for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: some uncertainty in the location and shape of objects represented by lines and points.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3.1.3 Evaluating Predictions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The most common metrics for evaluating road detection systems are precision and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: recall, which are known as correctness and completeness in the remote sensing litera-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ture [Wiedemann et al., 1998]. The precision is the fraction of predicted road pixels

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that are true roads , while the recall of a set of predictions is the fraction of true road

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pixels that were correctly detected.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Since the the vector maps we use to generate pixel labels are only accurate up

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to a few pixels we compute relaxed precision and recall scores instead of exact ones.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Namely, in our experiments recall represents the fraction of true road pixels that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are within

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pixels of a predicted road pixel, while precision represents the fraction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of predicted road pixels that are within

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pixels of a true road pixel. Relaxing the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: completeness and correctness measures in this manner is common practice when eval-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: uating road detection systems [Wiedemann et al., 1998]. The slack parameter

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: set to 3 pixels for all experiments performed in this thesis.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Since the methods presented in this thesis predict the probability of each label

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: belonging to the class of interest, it is possible to trade off precision for recall by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: varying the threshold for making a concrete prediction. One common way of evalu-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ating probabilistic binary classifiers is using precision-recall curves, which show the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: trade-off between precision and recall for all threshold values. We use precision-recall

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: curves for presenting quantitative comparisons involving a small number of models

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: because presenting entire curves conveys the most information.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: When making comparisons involving more than a few models, we opt for pre-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: senting plots or tables of summary statistics because precision-recall plots involving

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a large number of models can be difficult to interpret. While there are many well

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: known summary statistics for precision-recall curves, including

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: , breakeven

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: point, or precision at a fixed recall level, they all lose information compared to com-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: plete curves. However, we found that in our experiments sorting the models by their

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: performance on most reasonable summary statistics usually lead to the same order

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of models. This occurred because if one model achieved higher precision at one recall

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: level than another model it often achieved higher precision at all recall levels, domi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nating the other model. Due to this fact the choice of the summary statistic used to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: compare models was not particularly important because it had almost no impact on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the ordering of models. In the end we chose to report the point on the precision-recall

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: curve where precision is the same as recall, also known as the breakeven point, as the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: summary statistic. Figure 3.2 shows three precision-recall curves and their breakeven

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: points.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3.2 Datasets

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Due to the lack of aerial image datasets that are suitable for evaluating machine

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: learning methods, we constructed several large and challenging datasets using aerial

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 3. LEARNING TO LABEL AERIAL IMAGES

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: images of the Greater Toronto Area. We used these datasets for all experiments

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: performed in Chapters 3, 4, and 5. Unfortunately, the imagery used to construct these

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: datasets is not publicly available because we were not aware of several repositories

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of free high-resolution aerial imagery at the time. Chapter 6 will present the first

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: large-scale publicly available datasets for road and building detection along with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: benchmarks of the most promising models developed in this thesis. We now describe

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the characteristics of the proprietary datasets used in the next three chapters.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Toronto Roads Dataset

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The Toronto Roads dataset consists of roughly 500 square kilometers of training data,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 48 square kilometers of test data, and 8 kilometers of validation data at a resolution

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of 1.2m per pixel. This dataset contains both urban and suburban areas of Toronto.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The target road map for the Toronto Roads dataset contains some omitted roads but

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: has only minor registration problems.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Hamilton Roads Dataset

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The Hamilton Roads dataset consists of a training set of roughly 250 square kilometers

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the city of Hamilton at a resolution of 1.2m per pixel. The target road map for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: this dataset contains frequent registration errors in addition to some omitted roads

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and for this reason we only used it to study the effectiveness of the robust losses

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: introduced in Chapter 4. Figure 4.7(a) shows a representative subset of the Hamilton

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Roads dataset.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: GTA Buildings Dataset

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The GTA Building dataset consists of roughly 600 square kilometers of imagery of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the Greater Toronto Area. The target map contains significant omission errors and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: includes mostly large buildings, with most but not all houses unlabeled. Due to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: presence of noise in the targets, we used only 8 square kilometers of hand-labeled

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: data for validation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 3. LEARNING TO LABEL AERIAL IMAGES

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 3.3: Three sample input patches from the Toronto Roads dataset. The red

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: square denotes the region for which labels are predicted.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3.3 Architecture Evaluation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We now proceed to an evaluation of different neural network architectures on the task

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of road detection. We train the neural networks to predict 16 × 16 map patches from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: input aerial image patches in the Toronto Roads dataset. Figure 3.3 shows

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: three example input patches, with a red square denoting the region for which label

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predictions are to be made. In the Toronto Roads dataset each pixel corresponds to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1.44 square meters, making a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: input patch contain sufficient information for a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: human to correctly identify the objects in the target region.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We evaluate a number of architecture design choices, including the number of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: layers, the connectivity pattern between layers, types of hidden units, and the use of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pooling. While several such studies have been conducted for the problem of object

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: recognition [Jarrett et al., 2009, Coates et al., 2011] it is unclear whether the same

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conclusions apply for image labeling tasks. For example, max-pooling discards in-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formation about the location of features and while this may be beneficial for object

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: recognition it may not lead to similar improvements for image labeling, where the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: precise location of objects needs to be predicted. Moreover, due to the small size of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: most object recognition datasets design choices that help reduce overfitting seem to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: provide substantial benefits, but as we will see later in this chapter overfitting is far

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: less of a problem for our datasets so it is unclear whether methods that aim to reduce

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: overfitting will offer any benefits at all.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3.3.1 One Layer Architectures

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We first compare different neural networks with a single hidden layer. All the net-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: works we compare have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inputs that correspond to a contrast-normalized

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: RGB aerial image patch. The input is fed to a hidden layer that extracts roughly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 12000 features and applies a nonlinearity, possibly followed by pooling. The number

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of hidden units is held approximately the same in order to fix the size of the extracted

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: feature representation to be roughly the same. In all of the networks the hidden layer

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is followed by a fully connected output layer of 256 logistic output units. We compare

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the following one-layer architecture types differing only in the connectivity pattern of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the hidden layer:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Fully connected architecture: As the name suggests, this architecture has a fully

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: connected hidden layer. Since a fully connected network with 12000 hidden units has

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: roughly 150 million parameters it is slow to train even on a GPU. We instead use a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fully connected network with 4096 hidden units and roughly 50 million parameters,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: making it somewhat more manageable.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Factored architecture: The hidden layer of a factored architecture approximates

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a full

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: weight matrix as a dot product of two low rank matrices

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: where

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: U is an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: matrix and V is an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: matrix. This low rank approximation can

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: greatly reduce the number of free parameters over the full weight matrix. We use a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: factored hidden layer with 2048 factors f and 12000 hidden units. This architecture

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: has roughly the same number of parameters as the fully connected one but has three

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: times more hidden units.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Local untied architecture: The hidden layer of a locally connected architecture

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: drastically reduces the number of parameters over both fully connected and factored

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: architectures by only connecting each hidden unit to a small subpatch of the in-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: put. To precisely define the connectivity pattern, assume that the input units of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a locally connected layer make up a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: image consisting of multiple chan-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nels. The input image is divided into evenly spaced filter sites by moving a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: window over the image by a stride of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vertically and horizontally, for a total of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: filter sites. A different set of f filters of size

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consisting of the same number of channels as the input image is applied at each filter

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: site. Hence, a single locally connected layer results in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: input channels.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Convolutional architecture: The hidden layer of a convolutional architecture is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: simply a locally connected layer where the group of f filters applied at each location

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is the same. Restricting the filters to be the same at each location further reduces

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the number of parameters over a local untied architecture for a total of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ·C

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parameters.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Layer and unit types

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We first compare the different architecture types with two choices for the nonlinear-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ity/activation function in the hidden layer:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: • Logistic:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: • Rectified linear:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The local untied and convolutional architectures both used 12 × 12 filters and stride

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 4, while the other architectures are as described above. Table 3.2 shows the precision-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: recall breakeven points for the four architectures and activation functions. The recti-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fied linear (ReL) activation function clearly outperforms the logistic activation func-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion for all four architecture types. This result agrees with the findings of Jarrett

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: et al. [2009] and Nair and Hinton [2010] who reported substantial gains in perfor-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mance when using the ReL activation function on several object recognition tasks.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The best overall result is obtained by the convolutional architecture with ReL

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hidden units followed by the factored architecture with ReL units, which somewhat

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: surprisingly outperformed the local untied architecture. One possible explanation for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: this result is the fact that both the convolutional and factored architectures learn

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a shared set of filters over the input, which could make learning more statistically

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: efficient.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 3. LEARNING TO LABEL AERIAL IMAGES

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 3.4: Plots showing precision-recall breakeven points for (a) different pooling

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: regions, (b) different filter sizes in the first hidden layer.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Nevertheless, it is still surprising that, even though the only difference between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the convolutional and the local architecture is that the filters of the convolutional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: architecture are tied among all locations, the convolutional architecture substantially

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: outperforms the local architecture. We performed an additional experiment by ini-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tializing a local architecture with the weights of a convolutional architecture, which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corresponds to untying the weights of the convolutional architecture, and trained for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: three more epochs. Training the local architecture with this initialization resulted

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in a precision-recall breakeven point of 0.8695, which is an improvement over the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parameters used to initialize the model (0.8673). In comparison, training the convo-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lutional architecture for three more epochs without untying the weights improves the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: breakeven point from 0.8673 to 0.8713. These results suggest that the tied weights

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: make convolutional networks easier to optimize than untied local networks.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: While the above results show that the local untied architecture performed rela-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tively poorly, we will investigate it further along with the convolutional architecture

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the context of deep networks due to their computational efficiency when compared

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to the fully connected and factored architectures.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The effect of max pooling

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Max pooling has been shown to improve performance of convolutional architectures

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on a number of object recognition tasks [Jarrett et al., 2009] and we observe similar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: improvements for moderate amounts of pooling on both local untied and convolutional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 3. LEARNING TO LABEL AERIAL IMAGES

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: architectures on image labeling tasks. We evaluated the effects of max pooling when

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: placed on top of the hidden layers of local untied and convolutional architectures with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 64 filters of size 12 and stride 4. We compared pooling over overlapping regions of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: size

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with stride 1 The results shown in Figure

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: show

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that max pooling helps both untied local and convolutional architectures, with the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: best results obtained with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pooling regions. The fact that pooling over larger

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: regions leads to smaller improvements is not surprising given that the network needs

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to maintain precise locations of certain features.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The effects of filter sizes and strides

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We now look at the effect of filter size on the performance of local network archi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tectures. Figure 3.4(b) shows the precision-recall breakeven points for networks with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: filters of size 8, 12, 16, and 20 and filter stride 4. Both convolutional and untied

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: local networks seem to benefit from larger filter sizes, with larger improvements seen

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for untied local networks. This positive dependence on filter size is the opposite of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: what Coates et al. [2011] observed for unsupervised feature learning on object detec-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion tasks. It is unclear whether the difference is due to our use of supervised feature

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: learning, differing filter strides, or simply the type of data we use. Since Coates et al.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [2011] used a stride of 1 for the filter size experiments we investigated the possibility

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that smaller filters are better at smaller strides and found that this is not the case.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3.3.2 Two Layer Architectures

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We now turn to a similar analysis of two layer architectures of untied local and con-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: volutional layers with ReL hidden units. The first layer of both types of architectures

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: had 64 filters of size

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with stride 4. We investigated the effect of varying the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sizes of the filters and pooling regions in the second hidden layer.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The effect of max pooling

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We fixed the second layer of both architectures to have 128 4 × 4 filters with stride 1

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and then compared using no pooling,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: max pooling, and 3 × 3 max pooling on top

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the second layer. Figure 3.5(a) shows a plot of precision-recall breakeven points for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the different model configurations. Convolutional architectures do not seem to benefit

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from pooling in the second layer. Given that the first layer uses 3 max pooling, it is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 3. LEARNING TO LABEL AERIAL IMAGES

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 3.5: Plots showing precision-recall breakeven points for (a) different pooling

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: regions, (b) different filter sizes in the second hidden layer.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: likely that using any additional pooling in the second layer loses too much information

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: about the precise location of object parts to help on a pixel labeling task. Given this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: result, it is somewhat surprising that untied local architectures seem to benefit from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: max pooling in the second layer. As in the single hidden layer case, this effect is likely

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: explained by the fact that adding pooling to an untied local architecture encourages

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: filters in the same feature pool to be similar, with the resulting performance boost

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: outweighing the decrease in performance due to the lower spatial resolution.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The effects of filter sizes and strides

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We compared using filters of size 3, 4, 5, and 6 with stride 1 in the second layer of both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: architecture types. Figure 3.5(b) shows the precision-recall points for the different

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: model configurations. As in the single hidden layer case, larger filters seem to work

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: better in both types of architectures, with a more noticeable improvement for untied

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: local architectures. We also performed a control experiment to see whether using a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: smaller stride while holding the number of hidden units fixed improved results and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: found that, as in the one layer case, there was no significant change.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Discussion

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The local untied and convolutional architectures improve on the breakeven point for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a shallow factored model by more than 0.04 and 0.08 respectively while using far

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 3. LEARNING TO LABEL AERIAL IMAGES

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 3.6: A comparison of precision-recall curves for deep architectures. (a) A

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: comparison of different choices for the third layer of a deep architecture. (b). A

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: comparison of three, four and five layer networks.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fewer parameters. These results also show that increasing network depth clearly im-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proves the accuracy of untied and convolutional architectures on aerial image labeling

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tasks. Overall, convolutional architectures perform noticeably better than untied ar-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: chitectures suggesting that the ability to learn different filters at different locations

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is either not helpful or is far outweighed by the benefits of weight sharing found in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: convolutional nets.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3.3.3 Deeper Architectures

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Given the substantial improvements in precision and recall that we gained by adding

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a second layer to locally connected architectures we investigate whether adding even

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more layers helps. We start with a two layer convolutional network which has 64

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: filters and stride 4 in the first layer and 112 4 × 4 filters with stride 1 in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: second layer and add layers until it stops producing better results.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We compare three different choices for the third hidden layer: a fully connected

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: layer with 4096 hidden units, a factored layer with 2048 factors and 4096 hidden units,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and a convolutional layer with 80

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: filters and stride 1 for a total of 3920 hidden

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: units. The precision-recall plots for the three models as well as the base two layer

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: model are shown in Figure 3.6(a). There is a noticeable improvement in precision

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and recall from adding a third layer. The fully connected layer leads to the largest

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: improvement, but at the cost of using more parameters and computation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 3. LEARNING TO LABEL AERIAL IMAGES

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 3.7: Breakeven points for different settings of hyperparameters in a three

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: layer neural network on the Toronto Roads dataset. The green line indicates the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: performance of a three layer network with the default parameter values. (a) Different

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: learning rates € determined by the parameter k as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: With clear improvements from adding a third hidden layer we look into adding

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fourth and fifth layers. We use the model with three convolutional layers explored

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: above as the base model and compare adding a fully connected layer with 4096 hidden

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: units, a factored model with 4096 hidden units and 1024 factors, as well as two fully

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: connected layers with 4096 hidden units. Figure 3.6(b) shows the precision-recall

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: plots for these four layer models along with the base model. While there is a small

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: improvement in precision and recall from adding a fourth fully connected layer, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: improvement is small and adding a fifth layer actually hurts performance.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3.3.4 Sensitivity to Hyper Parameters

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In the above experiments, we did not perform a search over SGD and regularization

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hyperparameters and instead used parameter values that worked well for shallow net-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: works. While the deep networks exhibit good detection performance it is unclear how

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sensitive they are to these choices and whether performance can be further improved

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by tuning the hyperparameters. In order to address these questions, we performed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a sensitivity analysis for the three most important hyper parameters – the learning

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rate, the momentum, and the amount of weight decay.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figures 3.7(a), 3.7(b) 3.7(c) show the effects of varying the momentum, amount

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of weight decay, and learning rate on the precision-recall breakeven point of a three

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: layer network respectively. First, the plots show that the parameter choices that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: worked well for shallow networks translate relatively well to deep networks. The de-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 3. LEARNING TO LABEL AERIAL IMAGES

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 3.8: A plot showing training and validation log likelihoods on the Toronto

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Roads dataset at different points during training of a four layer neural network. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: gap between the two curves remains relatively constant even after 20 million training

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cases.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fault parameter value was always close to the best value tried on the deep network,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: suggesting that using shallow nets, which are much faster to train, for selecting hy-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perparmeter values is a sensible strategy. Second, the plots show that the results are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not overly sensitive to the values of hyperparameters, which means that, for a new

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dataset, trying a few values close to our suggested values could produce reasonable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: results.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3.3.5 A Word on Overfitting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Since overfitting is a common problem when training large neural networks, we de-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cided to investigate how severe it is for our models and data. In general, we found

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that even models with tens of millions of parameters do not seem to exhibit signif-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: icant overfitting when trained on our large datasets. Figure 3.8 shows training and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: validation log likelihoods at different points during training for a four layer neural

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: network trained on the Toronto Roads dataset. First, the validation log likelihood is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: always better than the training log likelihood because the relatively small validation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: set consists of relatively easy regions of the city. Second, the gap between training

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and validation curves is relatively constant throughout training suggesting that there

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is relatively little overfitting even after 22 million training cases have been processed.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3.4 Qualitative Evaluation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 3.9: Visualizations of neural network predictions on road and building detec-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion tasks. Green pixels are true positives, red pixels are false positives, blue pixels

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are false negatives, and background pixels are true negatives. Figures 3.9(a) and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3.9(b) show predictions on the Toronto Roads test set. Figures 3.9(c) and 3.9(d) are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predictions on the GTA Buildings test set.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 3. LEARNING TO LABEL AERIAL IMAGES

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We now apply the lessons learned in the previous section to training a large neural

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: network on road and building detection datasets. The network we train has four

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hidden layers. The first layer is convolutional with 64 filters of size 12 and stride

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 4, and is followed by size 3 stride 1 max pooling layer. The second hidden layer is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: convolutional with 112 filters of size 4 and stride 1 followed by another convolutional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: layer with 112 filters of size 3 and stride 1. The last hidden layer is fully connected and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: has 4096 hidden units. All four hidden layers use rectified linear units. We trained

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: two copies of this network on the Toronto Roads and GTA Buildings datasets. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: network trained on the Toronto Roads dataset achieved a breakeven point of 0.928

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on the test set, while the network trained on the GTA Buildings dataset achieved a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: breakeven point of 0.818 on its test data.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: To get some idea of what the numbers mean we visualize the predictions of both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: networks at their breakeven points. Figure 4.7 visualizes the predictions on parts

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the test set by colour coding each pixels based on whether it was a true or false

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: positive/negative, providing many interesting insights into how the networks work.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The predictions on the Toronto Roads dataset, shown in Figures 3.9(a) and 3.9(b),

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: demonstrate that the network is very good at detecting multiple types of roads includ-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ing two-lane roads in residential areas, multi-lane roads, and even highways. While

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the false positives and false negatives show several failure cases for our model, they

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also illustrate several problems with the data. For example, the network sometimes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: makes predictions for disconnected blobs of road in paved areas, which end up being

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: counted as false positives. This is an artifact of the network making independent pre-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dictions for each pixel, making it difficult for the network to realize that it is creating

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a disconnected component. Such errors can be avoided by incorporating structure

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: into the predictions and Chapter 5 examines different ways of doing so. Another

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: common type of mistake is a false negative caused by the shadow of a tall building.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: While we do not do so in this thesis, some form of local contrast normalization will

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: likely help in such cases.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We also see that the network is often penalized for making a road prediction in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: paved area. These predictions show up as false positives because narrow alleys and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: roads leading into malls or industrial areas are often not included in vector maps.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Whenever this type of mislabeling occurs in the training data the neural network is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: penalized for what is essentially a correct prediction.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The predictions for the network trained on the GTA Buildings dataset are shown

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 3. LEARNING TO LABEL AERIAL IMAGES

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 3.10: Visualizations of the input and output weights for a neural network

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: trained on a road detection task. (a) Convolutional filters from the first layer. (b).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Hidden to output weights for the 256 units with the largest weight norms.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in Figures 3.9(c) and 3.9(d). While the model is clearly not as good as our road

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: detector, there are a number of differences between the two tasks. First, building data,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: unlike road data, is almost always incomplete with as much as 30% of the buildings

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: left unlabeled, and there is simply less building data than road data. Additionally

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: there is much more variation in the shape and appearance of buildings than in roads.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Considering the quality of the data and the difficulty of the task, the neural network

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: still performs reasonably well.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The problems seen in the predictions of the building detector are similar to those

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: seen on road detection. For example, the false negatives that often appear in the mid-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dle of large buildings can be dealt with by incorporating structure in the predictions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Adding structure should also reduce false positives caused by predicted buildings with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: really improbable shapes. We will explore the use of structured prediction methods

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in Chapter 5.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3.4.1 Peering into the Mind of the Network

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: To gain some insight into what the network learns we first display the input and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: output weights learned by the network on the Toronto Roads dataset. Figure 3.10(a)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 3. LEARNING TO LABEL AERIAL IMAGES

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 3.11: Visualization of the derivatives of the loss function with respect to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: input pixel values.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shows all 64 convolutional filters from the first layer and 256 of the output filters with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the highest L2 norm. Not surprisingly, the convolutional filters the network learns are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: oriented edge and grating detectors, often with an overlaid lower frequency opposing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: yellow/blue and green/red patterns. Convolutional neural networks tend to learn

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: similar filters on other object detection tasks [Krizhevsky, 2011]. The output filters

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: learned by the network, shown in Figure 3.10(b), also exhibit interesting structure

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that falls into several groups. Two of the most prominent groups are entire road

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: segments at different orientations and filters that make a neutral prediction for much

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the patch and a strong vote for the absence of a road in one of the corners.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Another informative way of visualizing the neural network is through a sensitivity

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: analysis, which involves looking at the gradient of the loss function with respect to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the inputs at different data points. Figure 3.11 shows a number of input aerial image

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: patches from the Toronto Roads dataset with the squared gradient with respect to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the input for each data point overlaid in red. Hence, a change to the values of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: input pixels highlighted in red will cause a big change to the value of the loss function.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We see that whenever a piece of road is present in the centre 16 × 16 patch for which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the neural net is making predictions there is a strong gradient on the road pixels.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3.5 Conclusions and Discussion

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We have shown that our patch-based framework for learning to label aerial imagery

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with deep neural networks can achieve good performance on challenging real world

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: road and building detection datasets. The results show that there is a clear advantage

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to using deep networks over shallow ones and that convolutional networks outperform

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: networks with other types of connectivity. We also saw that while there is a bene-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 3. LEARNING TO LABEL AERIAL IMAGES

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fit from using a small amount of max pooling, using too much max pooling hurts

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: performance on pixel labeling tasks.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: While the framework addresses the basic problem of efficiently learning discrim-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inative features from large amounts of labeled aerial imagery, it has a number of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shortcomings. Most importantly, the neural network architectures we examined in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: this chapter make separate predictions for each pixel. As we saw in the previous

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: section, this leads to a number of undesirable artifacts in the predictions, including

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: disconnected blobs of road and gaps in roads and buildings. Chapter 5 will address

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the problem of how to efficiently incorporate rich structure into the predictions while

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: maintaining the ability to learn from very large datasets.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Another problem with the framework is the underlying assumption that the train-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ing data is perfectly labeled. Figure 4.7 clearly shows problems with the labels which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: likely hurt the neural networks during training. This issue has not been studied widely

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in machine learning or computer vision and Chapter 4 will attempt to modify our

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: learning procedure in ways that reduce the effects of noise typically found in maps

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on the neural networks.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In addition to addressing the above limitations there are many other ways to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: improve the performance of our system that we do not address in this thesis. One

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: interesting possibility is the use of losses other than negative log likelihood defined

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on individual label pixels. For example, Turaga et al. [2009] showed how directly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: optimizing a measure of image segmentation leads to much better segmentations

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: than by optimizing individual pixel disagreement. In our case, optimizing the area

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: under the precision-recall curve could lead to similar improvements because it is a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: better measure of the quality of the detections than log likelihood.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Another way of improving our system is by performing a more extensive hyperpa-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rameter search. While we have only looked at using a fixed learning rate and weight

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cost for all layers, using different values for each layer could both speed up learning

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and improve the overall performance. Since doing so requires searching over a very

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: large space of parameters, doing so by brute force search would require a tremendous

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: amount of computation. A more efficient way of performing this search is using the re-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cently developed methods for doing Bayesian global optimization of hyper parameter

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: values [Bergstra et al., 2011, Snoek et al., 2012].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Chapter 4

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Learning to Label from Noisy Data

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The preceding chapter demonstrated that it is possible to use readily available aerial

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: imagery along with vector metadata from sources such as OpenStreetMap to obtain

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: state-of-the-art performance on aerial image labeling tasks. While OpenStreetMap

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: provides an abundance of label information that is clearly of high-enough quality to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: learn from, the label information is often incomplete or noisy. In particular we classify

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the most common data inaccuracies into two types of noise:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: • Omission noise occurs when an object that appears in an aerial image does

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not appear in the map. This is the case for many buildings (even in major cities)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: due to incompleteness of the maps. It is also true for small roads and alleys,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which tend to be omitted from maps, often with no clear criterion for when they

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: should be omitted. An example of omission noise is shown in Figure 4.1(a).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: • Registration noise occurs when the location of an object in a map is inaccu-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rate. Such errors are quite common because not requiring pixel level accuracy

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: makes maps cheaper to produce for human experts without significantly re-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ducing their usefulness for most purposes. An example of registration noise is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shown in Figure 4.1(b)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The presence of these kinds of errors in the training labels can significantly reduce

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the accuracy of classifiers trained on such data.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: This chapter shows how one can deal with the presence of both kinds of noise in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: training labels. We present two robust loss functions that can be incorporated into our

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: image labeling framework. The first loss function reduces the effect of omission errors

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 4. LEARNING TO LABEL FROM NOISY DATA

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 4.1: Road locations derived from a map are shown in red. (a) Example of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: 4.1 Dealing With Omission Noise

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Omission noise, as shown in Figure 4.1(a), occurs when some map pixels are labeled

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as not belonging to the object class of interest when they, in fact, do. When trained

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on data containing a substantial number of such pixels a classifier will be penalized

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for correctly predicting the value of 1 for pixels affected by omission noise. This will

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cause a classifier to be less confident and potentially increase the false negative rate.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We propose using a robust loss function that explicitly models asymmetric omis-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sion noise in order to reduce its effect on the final classifier. We recall that in Chapter 3

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the observed map distribution

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was modeled directly by a neural network. By

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the training data consists of true samples from a model in this class of models. In

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 4.2.3 Understanding the Noise Model

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In order to demonstrate how the translational noise model works in practice, we used

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the TABN model to train a neural network to detect roads from poorly registered

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: road data and plot the target labels, the model predictions, and the inferred true

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: labels for several test cases. Figure 4.4 shows target map labels in the top row, model

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predictions in the middle row, and means of the marginals of the true map posterior

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the bottom row. These examples show how the TABN model is able to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: correctly realign the target map with the aerial images.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 4.3 Results

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 4.3.1 Omission Noise

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We begin by evaluating the effectiveness of the ABN noise model on the Toronto

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Roads and GTA Buildings datasets. We estimate that the omission rate is less than

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 4. LEARNING TO LABEL FROM NOISY DATA

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 4.4: Demonstration of the translational noise model on road detection data.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 5% on the Toronto Roads dataset and roughly 30% on the GTA buildings dataset

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: so we expect to see some improvement from using a noise model. While the GTA

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Buildings test set was hand-corrected to include buildings missing from the source

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: map, the Toronto Roads test set was not. We decided to not hand correct the Toronto

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Roads test set because it is not entirely clear what should and should not be labeled

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as a road. Since omission noise can potentially lead to worse predictions on all data,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it should still be possible for a noise model to improve performance even on a noisy

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: test set.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We trained three layer networks on both datasets with both the ABN model and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the noise free model. Since the aim of using the ABN model is to improve robustness

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to omission noise we apply the ABN model only on training cases where the target

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: map patch m is blank, meaning that all the labels are 0, and use the noise free model

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for all non-blank training cases. By avoiding non-blank patches, which are much less

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: likely to contain omission errors than blank ones, this procedure helps reduce errors

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: where a noise model incorrectly overrules the ground truth on non-blank patches.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Road Data

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: While our earlier work [Mnih and Hinton, 2012] showed a clear improvement from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: using a noise model on the Toronto Roads dataset, we have since discovered that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the improvement cannot be directly attributed to the use of a noise model. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: true difference in performance can be explained by the fact that the noise free model

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 4. LEARNING TO LABEL FROM NOISY DATA

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: trained on the GTA Buildings dataset.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: used soft labels generated using the procedure described in Chapter 3 while the ABN

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: model required binarized labels. Figure 4.5(a) shows precision-recall plots on the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Toronto Roads test set for the ABN model as well as the noise free model with both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: soft and binarized labels. Using the noise free model with binarized labels instead

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of soft labels leads to almost the same performance as using the ABN model, with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: breakeven points of 0.9179 and 0.9181 respectively.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: It is not immediately clear why there is no noticeable improvement in precision

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and recall from using a noise model on this data. Is it because the noise model does

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not work or because the noise is not very harmful? In order to answer this question

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: we conduct a number of experiments on the Toronto Roads dataset with synthetic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: omission noise. We generated three versions of the Toronto Roads training set by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dividing it into non-overlapping 500 by 500 meter regions and randomly deleting all

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: labels in 10, 20, or 40 percent of these regions respectively. This type of structured

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noise is a good approximation to unmapped regions often found in OpenStreetMap

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: data.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We then proceeded to train the same three layer network used in the preceding

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ABN model experiments on the three versions of the dataset with the noise free and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ABN models. The first row of Table 4.1 shows precision-recall breakeven points for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the noise free model under varying amounts of label noise. Somewhat surprisingly,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: our neural network models seem to be quite robust to the presence of omission noise

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Since according to our estimates the uncorrupted Toronto Roads dataset has an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Nevertheless, since the difference on uncorrupted data is so small, we also evaluate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the ABN noise model on the corrupted datasets to see how much of the decrease our

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Building Data

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 4.5(b) shows the precision-recall plots for the noise free and ABN models

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on the hand-corrected GTA Buildings test set. Using the ABN model on the GTA

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Buildings dataset improves the precision-recall breakeven point by roughly 0.085.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The improvement is a much larger than what we saw on the Toronto Roads dataset

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: because the GTA Buildings training set has a much higher omission rate of roughly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 30%. Given that the results in the previous section suggest that neural networks

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: trained with the noise free loss are quite robust to omission noise the improvement

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on this data underscores the effectiveness of the ABN noise model.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 4.3.2 Registration Noise

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In order to evaluate the robustness of the TABN model to registration noise, we per-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form experiments on the Hamilton Roads dataset. While the Toronto data contains

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relatively few registration problems, with most road labels within one or two meters

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the true locations, road centerlines in the Hamilton Roads dataset are often more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: than 5 meters away from their true locations. We train the ABN and TABN models

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on the Hamilton training set and evaluate them on the Toronto Roads test set because

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it is much cleaner.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 4.6 shows precision-recall curves on the Toronto Roads test set for the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: models trained on the Hamilton training set and demonstrates the clear advantage of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: using the TABN robust loss function on this data. In addition to the TABN model,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: we include results for the ABN model, as well as a noise free model trained on both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: soft and binarized labels. As we saw on the road data, much of the improvement of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the ABN model over the noise free model can be attributed to using binarized labels.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Nevertheless, we get a substantial improvement in the precision recall curve from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: training a network with the TABN model, improving the precision-recall breakeven

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: point by 0.0176 when compared to the ABN model.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: It might seem surprising that the improvement from using the TABN model is so

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: much higher than from using the ABN model even on data with a lot of synthetic

layout_dets.label: display_formula
layout_dets.latex: p ( \tilde { \mathbf { m } } | \mathbf { m } , \mathbf { s } , t ) = \prod _ { i = 1 } ^ { w _ { m } ^ { 2 } } p _ { A B N } ( \tilde { m } _ { i } | G ( \mathbf { m } , t ) _ { i } ) ,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: omission noise. The improvement is likely explained by two factors. First, neural

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: networks are likely less robust to registration errors than omission errors because while

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: omission errors may simply reduce the confidence of the neural network's predictions,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: registration errors can result in learning encouraging predictions that are entirely

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: wrong. The second factor explaining the effectiveness of the translational noise model

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is the fact that under truly local registration errors it is possible for the TABN model

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perfectly recover the true labels by translating the observed labels.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We further demonstrate the robustness of the TABN model to registration noise

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by visualizing its predictions on noisy training data. Figure 4.7(a) shows an area

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from the Hamilton Roads training set with the ground truth road locations overlaid

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in red while Figure 4.7(b) shows the predictions of a model trained with the TABN

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: loss for the same area of the training set. The alignment between the predicted road

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: locations and their true locations is clearly much better than it is for the training

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: labels even though the training labels are what the model was trained to predict.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 4.4 Conclusions and Discussion

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We have shown that by using robust loss functions to train neural networks instead

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the standard negative log likelihood loss can provide some level of robustness to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: label noise. Somewhat surprisingly, large amounts of omission noise do not seem

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to significantly hurt the training of deep neural networks without a noise model,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: although our ABN noise model does show across-the-board improvements. We also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: saw that while the more structured registration noise is more harmful when no noise

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: model is used, it is actually easier to deal with when a translational noise model is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: used.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: While our noise models were designed specifically for the types of noise one faces

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in aerial image labeling tasks, they can be easily modified to handle other types of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noise. For example, the translational noise model can be generalized to handle any

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: type of label noise for which we can write down a graphics program parameterized

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with a single discrete transformation variable t. Any such graphics program

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: leads to a noise distribution

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 4. LEARNING TO LABEL FROM NOISY DATA

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that gives us some robustness to the transformation G. Rotations and shears are two

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: basic examples of transformations that can be handled in this manner.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: One interesting extension of the ABN model is the addition of dependencies be-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tween pixels of the unobserved true map M. This modification would allow strong

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: disagreements with the ground truth in one part of a patch to influence weaker dis-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: agreements in nearby parts of the patch. One way to achieve this effect is by placing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an MRF prior on M, leading to a combination of a CRF and our ABN noise model.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We will show how this model can be trained efficiently in the next chapter.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 4. LEARNING TO LABEL FROM NOISY DATA
