layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Chapter 5

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Structured Prediction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: So far we have only used unstructured models, meaning ones in which predictions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for individual pixels do not directly influence each other. Even though unstructured

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: models seem to be capable of achieving good performance on the tasks we have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: considered, incorporating knowledge about the smoothness or shape of the predicted

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: objects should lead to even better performance. Indeed, as we discussed in Chapter 2,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: incorporating structure into aerial and general image labeling methods has often led

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to big improvements in accuracy and can be traced back to some of the earliest work

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on the subject [Kettig and Landgrebe, 1976, Bischof et al., 1993, He et al., 2004,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Kluckner et al., 2009].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: To gain some insight into the kinds of issues that we hope to address by incorporat-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ing structure we show sample predictions on the Toronto Roads and GTA Buildings

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: datasets in Figures 5.1(a) and 5.1(b) respectively. On road data, the most common

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: problems are disconnected blobs of road and gaps in the predicted road network.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A model that incorporates a connectedness constraint on the road network should

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be able to avoid both types of errors. Similarly, the most common issues found in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predicted building maps are holes and disconnected blobs. Unlike with road data,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: however, shape and layout are the cues that must be used to resolve these types of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: errors. Incorporating structure into an image labeling approach by placing a smooth-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ness prior over the labels is likely to help address the issues with both road and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: building detection. On top of this, incorporating higher level information, such as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shape, is likely to lead to further gains.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In this chapter, we aim to address the problem of incorporating rich dependencies

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: among the outputs of our models without sacrificing the ability to learn from large

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 5. STRUCTURED PREDICTION

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 5.1: Sample predictions for a base network on the Toronto Roads and GTA

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Buildings datasets.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: datasets and deal with noisy labels. We first show how stacking neural networks on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: top of each other indirectly introduces high-level dependencies between the outputs.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Training a neural network to clean up the predictions of another neural network in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: this manner makes it easier to incorporate knowledge about shape into resulting the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predictions. We then show how post-processing neural networks can be extended to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: post-processing Conditional Random Fields by adding direct pairwise dependencies

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between the outputs of the neural network. Adding direct pairwise dependencies

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: makes it easier for the models to capture low-level properties such as smoothness.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The resulting models lead to substantial improvements in precision and recall over

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: our unstructured models.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 5.1 Post-processing Neural Networks

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Given that our goal is to incorporate structure into our models without sacrificing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the benefits of fast online training and noise models, perhaps the easiest way to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accomplish this is by recycling our existing machinery for training neural networks.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: While the neural networks we have been using do not have explicit dependencies

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between the outputs, indirect dependencies can be introduced by stacking several

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: neural networks, each using the outputs of the previous neural network as its inputs.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We make use of our patch-based prediction framework using patches of predictions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 5. STRUCTURED PREDICTION

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 5.2: A stack of two post-processing neural networks.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: instead of patches of aerial images as input. We will refer to neural networks taking

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: patches of predictions instead of aerial images as input as post-processing or cleanup

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: neural networks.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: To precisely define the setup, let

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be the map predicted from an aerial image by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one of the models described in the preceding chapters. The ith level post-processing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: neural network

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: takes a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: patch of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and outputs a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: patch of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: . As with the other neural network models,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is trained to minimize the negative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: log probability of patches of the observed map

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Hence, the ith post-processing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: neural network aims to improve on the predictions of the previous neural network

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: . Figure 5.2 shows a stack of two such post-processing neural networks.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Each post-processing neural network should be able to improve or match the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: quality of the predictions of the previous network for two reasons. First, the fact that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the network trained to predict a set of labels from a set of predictions for this set of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: labels should allow it to at least match the accuracy of the preceding neural network.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: It should also be easier to represent dependencies between predictions than in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: network that is trying to predict the same labels from an aerial image patch. Second,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by using an input patch larger than the output patch, each successive network is using

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 5. STRUCTURED PREDICTION

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 5.3: Predictions of post-processing neural networks for the areas shown in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 5.1.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: information extracted from a larger and larger area of the aerial image as input. This

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: allows post processing networks to propagate confidence along the predicted maps.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: There are two main advantages to using post-processing neural networks for in-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corporating structure into the predictions. One immediate benefit is the fact that the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: robust losses from Chapter 4 can be used to train post-processing networks without

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: modification. Two, given the fact that neural networks are universal approxima-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tors, at least in theory, post-processing neural networks are capable of representing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: arbitrary dependencies between input predictions and output label probabilities.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: As we discussed in Chapter 2, trained classifiers have been used for post-processing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the past. For example, Bischof et al. [1993] trained logistic regression models to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: remove salt and pepper noise from aerial image classification results. In the remainder

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of this section, we evaluate different types of post-processing neural network archi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tectures, including shallow, single hidden layer networks and networks with multiple

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: levels of local or convolutional features, on road and building detection tasks. Our

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: results confirm the effectiveness of this simple approach to doing structured predic-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 5.1.1 Results

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: To evaluate different post-processing neural network architectures, we first trained

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: two copies of a three layer locally connected network on the Toronto Roads and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: GTA Buildings datasets. These base networks used aerial image patches as input

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the base networks on each dataset.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The first architecture is a neural network with a single fully-connected hidden

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figures 5.4(a) and 5.4(b) show the precision-recall curves for the models we com-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: post-processing network architectures give a substantial improvement in precision

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: themselves is quite small. We found this to be a general trend – post processing leads

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to a substantial improvement over the base network, but there is little difference in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: performance between different architecture choices such as the sizes and types of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hidden layers.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In order to visually demonstrate the improvement in the predictions of the post-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: processing networks over the base networks, Figure 5.3 shows the predictions of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: best post-processing networks on the areas for which base network predictions are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shown in Figure 5.1. The post-processing network suppressed the disconnected blobs

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of road present in the base network predictions in Figure 5.1(a) and filled in most of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the gaps in the road network. The network essentially learns to propagate confident

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predictions along the map while respecting the constraints of the predicted road

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: network. A similar effect can be seen in the building predictions, where the post-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: processing network propagates confident predictions while respecting the constraints

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on building shape it has learned from the data.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 5.2 Conditional Random Fields

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: One drawback of post-processing neural networks is that they do not incorporate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prior knowledge by explicitly coupling the model outputs and instead attempt to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: learn all dependencies from data. While, as we showed in the previous section, this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: approach is able to learn useful dependencies between outputs, post processing neural

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: networks fail to model local smoothness, which is the strongest local dependence.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Though stacking multiple post-processing neural networks on top of one another

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: might eventually come close to modeling smoothness really well, it may be easier and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more effective to incorporate such strong prior knowledge directly into the model.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In this section, we explore extending our deep neural networks to deep Conditional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Random Fields (CRFs) by adding explicit dependencies between outputs of a neural

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: network. In particular, we add a smoothness term between neighbouring pixels to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: our model, removing the need to learn smoothness from the data. Using the resulting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: models for post-processing leads to substantial improvements over unstructured, post-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: processing neural networks.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: This basic pairwise CRF model can be extended in a number of different ways. For

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: example, Kohli et al. [2009] build a model that combines multiple oversegmentations of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the model could conceivably be able to reason about the relative locations of predicted

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: objects whenever it is used for post-processing. We also hope that the use of a deep

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: While the problem of finding the MAP labeling in general CRFs, known as MAP

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inference, is known to be NP-hard, there are broad classes of CRFs for which efficient

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: exact MAP inference is possible. Pairwise CRFs in which the pairwise potentials

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: satisfy a condition known as submodularity are one such class. Under our formulation,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: submodularity corresponds to the condition

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: For any model satisfying this condition, the MAP labeling can be found in polynomial

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: time using graph cuts [Greig et al., 1989]. Conveniently, the submodularity condition

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: simply states that the model should favour smoothness in the labels and it is satisfied

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by our models for all non-positive values of α.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Despite the fact that efficient and exact MAP inference for our model is possible

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: using graph cuts, it is not a good choice in this setting because it produces a hard

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: labeling. The resulting labeling leads to a single pair of precision and recall values,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: making it impossible to trade off one for the other by choosing a threshold. Indeed, we

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: found that graph cut inference leads to predictions with high precision and moderate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: recall, which may not be desirable. For this reason, we do not use MAP inference

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and instead perform marginal inference where the goal is to compute the marginals

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for all pixels i. Computing the marginals allows us to trade off precision

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and recall against each other by choosing a threshold and using it to produce a hard

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: assignment from the marginal probabilities.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inference led to nearly identical precision-recall curves, mean field inference is both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: faster and more straight forward to implement, so we present it here in detail.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: operator of the Markov chain we used for our model is a block Gibbs sampler with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: two groups defined using a checker board pattern, as shown in Figure 5.5. All the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shaded nodes can be updated in parallel given all the unshaded nodes and vice versa,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: allowing us to update all nodes in just two block Gibbs updates. By running the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Markov chain until it reaches equilibrium, we could obtain samples from the model

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: p(m|s) and use them to approximate the negative term expectation. Unfortunately

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: this approach is impractical because it takes a long time to reach equilibrium.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: One alternative is to use Contrastive Divergence (CD) learning [Hinton, 2002],

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which initializes the Markov chain at the data m and runs the Markov chain for a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: small number of steps instead of running until convergence. We found that finetuning

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a CRF using CD actually made the predictions worse. This confirms our earlier

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: finding that CD may not work well for training conditional models [Mnih et al., 2011]

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: where the Markov chain mixes slowly. Intuitively, CD training lowers the energy of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the observed data and raises the energy of the regions near the true data. This may

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not work well for a conditional model because test time inference starts away from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the true data and may never reach the regions of the state space explored by CD at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: training time.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We experimented with a number of alternatives to standard CD training and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: found that we could successfully finetune a CRF using CD where the Markov chain

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the negative phase run at temperature 2 instead of 1. Running the Markov chain

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at the higher temperature improved mixing in the chain. Additionally, we found that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: using a different value of the pairwise smoothness penalty term α at training time also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: improved mixing of the chain leading to even better finetuning results. While using

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the value of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: works well at test time, it leads to rather rigid smoothness

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constraints on the labels which make it difficult for our Gibbs sampler to make large

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: moves. Thus our finetuning procedure used CD with the negative chain running at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: temperature 2 for 5 steps and the pairwise penalty term set to -0.6. While it might

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be possible to use CD training without any model modifications by using a better

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sampler such as Swendsen-Wang [Swendsen and Wang, 1987], we did not explore this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: possibility.

layout_dets.text: 5.2.4 Results

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Due to the fact that smoothness is more important for building detection than road

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: detection we evaluate the proposed CRF model on the GTA Buildings dataset. We

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: evaluate two types of models – base models taking aerial images as input and post-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: processing models using the outputs of a neural network as the input.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dataset for neural networks as well as CRFs trained in different ways. NN denotes a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: deep neural network trained using the procedure described in Chapter 3, while CRF

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: denotes a CRF whose neural network weights were initialized with the weights of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: NN. The parameters of this model were not finetuned. The model Finetuned CRF

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: epochs by optimizing the CRF likelihood using Contrastive Divergence. Finally, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: model Finetuned NN CRF is a CRF whose neural network weights were obtained

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by training NN for two more epochs using the standard neural net likelihood. We

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: included Finetuned NN CRF to see if there is a benefit from finetuning a CRF using

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the CRF likelihood as opposed to just training the neural network part longer using

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the unstructured neural network likelihood.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CRFs trained using all three procedures substantially outperform NN. For both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: base and post-processing models, simply placing an MRF over the outputs of a neural

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: network to turn it into a CRF, which is the difference between NN and CRF, improves

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: precision-recall breakeven points by roughly 0.015. We also see that while finetuning a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: than simply training the neural network longer, the difference between these two

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: methods is too small to be conclusive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: It is also interesting to note that post-processing CRFs are the best performing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: models, outperforming both post processing neural networks and base CRFs. This

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: suggests that the improvements from doing post-processing with a neural net and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: directly incorporating smoothness using a CRF are somewhat orthogonal and that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In order to better understand how adding pairwise dependencies changes the pre-

layout_dets.text: dataset that is covered by Figure 5.1(b). First, it is evident that the CRFs produce

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 5.3 Combining Structure and Noise Models

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In this section, we combine the Asymmetric Binary Noise model we developed in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Chapter 4 with the deep CRFs presented in Section 5.2. The combination of these

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: models is especially interesting because the pixel-by-pixel ABN noise model should

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: become more powerful when used to train a CRF. In particular, using the ABN model

layout_dets.label: display_formula
layout_dets.latex: p ( \tilde { \mathbf { m } } | \mathbf { s } ) = \sum _ { \mathbf { m } } \left( \prod _ { i } p ( \tilde { \mathbf { m } } _ { i } | \mathbf { m } _ { i } ) \right) p ( \mathbf { m } | \mathbf { s } ) .

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 5. STRUCTURED PREDICTION

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to train a CRF should allow nearby disagreements of the neural network predictions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with the ground truth to reinforce each other. This effect does not exist when the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ABN model is used to train a neural network because the negative log likelihood

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: decomposes over pixels due to the lack of direct dependencies between different labels.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 5.3.1 The model

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We recall from Chapter 4 that in order to deal with omission noise we defined the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: following two-stage generative model of the data:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1. Generate the true, uncorrupted and unobserved map m from the aerial image

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: s according to a data distribution

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2. Generate the corrupted observed map ñ from the true map m according to a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noise distribution

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: When the noise distribution is specified by the asymmetric binary noise model, this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generative process leads to the following observed map distribution:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In Chapter 4, the true map distribution

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was specified using a neural net and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: factored over pixels, which led to a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that also factored over pixels. Here, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: true map distribution is specified by a CRF, which means that the observed map

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distribution no longer factors over pixels. We will refer to this model as the CRF-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ABN model. While coupling the pixels in this manner makes learning more difficult,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it gives the model some interesting properties. Figure 5.8 shows the difference in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inferred true map m between the ABN and CRF-ABN models. In particular, one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: can see how nearby disagreements reinforce each other in the CRF-ABN model and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not in the ABN model.

layout_dets.text: 5.3.3 Learning

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: As the CRF-ABN model can be seen as a latent CRF with a stationary pixelwise

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: emission distribution, we will use the EM algorithm to optimize the log likelihood

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the presence of latent variables. As in our application of the EM algorithm to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the translational noise model, we are not able to perform a full M-step and instead

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perform a partial approximate one by doing a single minibatch gradient update.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: However, unlike in the case of the translational noise model, we are no longer able

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to perform an exact E-step because expectations with respect to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tractable under the CRF-ABN model. Instead, we chose to perform a variational

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E-step, where we use a fully factored mean field approximation q(m) in place of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: . We found that this scheme works well in practice.

layout_dets.text: 5.3.4 Results

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We evaluate both proposed procedures for training the CRF-ABN model on the GTA

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Buildings dataset using and compare it to the performance of a CRF trained using the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CRF likelihood. Table 5.2 shows precision-recall breakeven points for three different

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: settings. CRF corresponds to training a CRF by maximizing the CRF likelihood with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Contrastive Divergence while CRF-ABN corresponds to using the training criterion for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CRF-ABN based on variational EM. The third line CRF-ABNNN corresponds to using

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the alternative training criterion for the CRF-ABN model.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The CRF-ABN model outperforms training with the standard CRF likelihood for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: both base and post-processing networks, although the improvement is larger for post-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: processing networks. It is possible that some of the omission errors are predictable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from the input aerial image but not from a patch of predictions. The presence of such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: regularities in the omission noise would explain the larger improvement from training

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a post-processing network with a noise model.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 5.3.5 Discussion

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: This chapter presented two effective and complementary ways of incorporating struc-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ture into the outputs of our image labeling system. Adding direct pairwise dependen-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cies between neighbouring labels predicted by a neural network helps produce smooth

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: labelings. We also showed that training a neural network or a CRF using the outputs

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of a neural network as input helps it indirectly capture higher-order dependencies

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between outputs. The combination of the two approaches, namely using a CRF to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clean up the predictions of a neural network is particularly effective at capturing both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: low-level and high-level dependencies.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Overall, we saw that, on the GTA Buildings dataset, training a post-processing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CRF using a noise model improved the precision-recall breakeven point over a using

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: just a deep neural network by roughly 0.04. Given that the deep neural network is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 5. STRUCTURED PREDICTION

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: already a powerful model, the improvement is substantial.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: There are a number of interesting extensions of the proposed models. One promis-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ing direction is to investigate the use of pairwise potentials that are modulated by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a neural network instead of a simple image-dependent term. Given that we found it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: necessary to use image-dependent pairwise potentials in order to get an improvement

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from using a CRF we believe that making this part of the model more powerful could

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lead to substantial improvements. The promising results obtained on several image

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: labeling tasks in Jancsary et al. [2012] using a model where the pairwise potentials

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are determined using regression trees provide further evidence.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Large-Scale Evaluation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: So far, we have presented a complete framework for learning to label aerial images, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: while we have provided experimental validation along the way, we have not directly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: compared our results to the work of others. As we discussed in Chapter 2, the rarity

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of direct comparisons between proposed aerial image interpretation methods is a long-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: standing problem in the area and we believe that it is primarily caused by the lack

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of high quality publicly available aerial image datasets. In this chapter, we introduce

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the first large-scale and publicly available road and building detection datasets, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: evaluate the most promising methods from the rest of the thesis on the new datasets.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We hope that the availability of these new high-quality datasets will both facilitate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more comparisons of existing methods and lead to increased interest in aerial imagery

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: applications in the machine learning and computer vision communities. Furthermore,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the evaluation of methods presented in this thesis on challenging datasets that were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not used during the development of these methods offers further validation of their

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: effectiveness.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We have assembled three datasets using publicly available imagery and metadata.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Two of the datasets make use of imagery released by the state of Massachusetts 1

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: while the third dataset uses imagery released by the state of New York 2. All imagery

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was rescaled to a resolution of 1 pixel per square meter. The target maps for all three

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: datasets were generated using data from the OpenStreetMap project. Target maps

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for the test and validation portions of all three datasets were hand-corrected to make

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 6.1 Massachusetts Buildings Dataset

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The Massachusetts Buildings Dataset consists of 151 aerial images of the Boston

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: area, with each of the images being 1500 × 1500 pixels for an area of 2.25 square

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: kilometers. Hence, the entire dataset covers roughly roughly 340 square kilometers.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We randomly split the data into a training set of 137 images, a test set of 10 images and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a validation set of 4 images. The target maps were obtained by rasterizing building

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: footprints obtained from the OpenStreetMap project. Unlike the GTA Buildings

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dataset we have used throughout the thesis, this data was restricted to regions with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an average omission noise level of roughly 5% or less. It was possible to collect such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a large a mount of high quality building footprint data because the City of Boston

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: has contributed building footprints for the entire city to the OpenStreetMap project.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The dataset covers mostly urban and suburban areas and buildings of all sizes,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: including individual houses and garages, are included in the labels. Figures 6.1(a)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and 6.1(b) show two representative regions from the Massachusetts Buildings dataset.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 6.2 Massachusetts Roads Dataset

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The Massachusetts Roads Dataset consists of 1171 aerial images of the state of Mas-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sachusetts. As with the building data, each image is 1500 × 1500 pixels in size, covering

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an area of 2.25 square kilometers. We randomly split the data into a training set of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1108 images, a validation set of 14 images and a test set of 49 images. The dataset

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: covers a wide variety of urban, suburban, and rural regions and covers an area of over

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2600 square kilometers. With the test set alone covering over 110 square kilometers,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: this is by far the largest and most challenging aerial image labeling dataset. Fig-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ures 6.2(a) and 6.2(b) show two representative regions from the Massachusetts Roads

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dataset.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The target maps were generated by rasterizing road centerlines obtained from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the OpenStreetMap project. We used a line thickness of 7 pixels and no smoothing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: because, as we discovered in Chapter 4, using hard binary labels for training works

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: better than using soft binary labels.

layout_dets.text: 6.4 Results

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 6.4.1 Massachusetts Datasets

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The main model we evaluated on the Massachusetts datasets is a large convolutional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: neural network. The input to the model is a 64 by 64 aerial image patch. The first

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hidden layer is a convolution layer with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: filters with stride 4. It is followed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: max pooling with stride 1. The second hidden layer is also convolutional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with 112 filters of size

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with stride 1, followed by a third convolutional layer with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 80 filters of size

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with stride 1. The fourth, and final, hidden layer is a fully

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: connected layer with 4096 hidden units. All four hidden layers consist of rectified

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: linear units. As before, the output layer is a fully-connected layer of 256 logistic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: units.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The neural network was trained using stochastic gradient descent with minibatches

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of size 128 using the hyper-parameter values described in Chapter 3. Additionally,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: after every

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: training cases, we multiplied the learning rate by 0.95. Training

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stopped after

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cases had been processed.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We evaluated two other methods in addition to the plain neural network – a CRF

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: initialized with the neural network weights, and a post-processing network trained

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sachusetts Buildings dataset. Figures 6.3(c) and 6.3(d) show predictions of a post-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: processing network on these regions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on the outputs of the base neural network. We did not tune the value of the CRF's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pairwise interaction term α and simply used the value -1.2 because it worked well

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on the GTA Buildings dataset. The post-processing neural network had one fully-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Table 6.1: Precision-recall breakeven points for different models on the Massachusetts

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: datasets.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Table 6.1 shows the precision-recall breakeven points on the Massachusetts datasets

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for the three models described above. We see that there is a relatively small improve-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ment from using a CRF on both datasets and that post-processing neural networks

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: outperform CRFs on road data. It is surprising that the improvement obtained by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structured models on the building data is quite small compared to the improvement

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: obtained on the GTA Buildings dataset. The main difference between the datasets

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is that the Massachusetts Buildings dataset is dominated by individual houses while

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the GTA Buildings dataset consists almost entirely of larger buildings. It is possible

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that the gain from structured prediction on the Massachusetts data is smaller because

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure is not as important for detecting small objects such as houses.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: To get a better idea of how well these models work, we include visualizations of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predictions of the post-processing networks on test data from both datasets. Fig-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ures 6.1(c) and 6.1(d) show predictions of the post-processing neural network trained

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on the building data for the regions shown in Figures 6.1(a) and 6.1(b). The network

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is very good at detecting individual houses but does less well on larger buildings.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: This is not entirely surprising because there is significantly more variation in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: appearance of large buildings and the model saw fewer of them during training Fig-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ures 6.2(c) and 6.2(d) show predictions of the post-processing neural network trained

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on the Massachusetts Roads dataset. As these results show, the model is very good

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at detecting roads in a variety of settings and even under significant occlusions by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: trees.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 6.4.2 Buffalo Roads Dataset

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The Buffalo Roads dataset was constructed in order to evaluate how well models

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: trained on the Massachusetts Roads dataset generalize to substantially different con-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ditions. Table 6.2 shows the precision-recall breakeven points for a number of different

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 6. LARGE-SCALE EVALUATION

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: models on the Buffalo Roads test set. NN Mass corresponds to the big convolutional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: neural network trained on the Massachusetts data and this model clearly works poorly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on the Buffalo data. NN Buffalo corresponds to the same convolutional architecture,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: but trained on the small Buffalo Roads training set. While this model works surpris-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ingly well given that it was trained on less than 3 square kilometers of imagery, it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: still achieves a breakeven point of just 0.7960.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Comparing images from the Massachusetts (Figures 6.2(a) and 6.2(b)) and Buffalo

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (Figures 6.3(a) and6.3(b)) datasets suggests that the main difference may be in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distribution of colours and that the structure of the roads may be largely the same.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Using this hypothesis as motivation we evaluated several ways of adapting the network

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: trained on Massachusetts data to Buffalo data using the small training set.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: One straightforward way of compensating for the difference in colour distribution

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between the datasets is by transforming the Buffalo data to have the same colour

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: histogram as the Massachusetts data. The third model from Table 6.2 corresponds to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: running the NN Mass model on colour corrected Buffalo data. This simple strategy

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: requires only unlabeled data and turns out to be reasonably effective, as it boosts

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the breakeven-point from 0.5613 to 0.8099. The other strategy for adapting the NN

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Mass model to the Buffalo data involves using the small training set to finetune the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: weights of the model. We started with the weights of NN Mass, trained it on the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Buffalo Roads training set for 128 epochs using a learning rate of 10−4, and saved the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: weights that gave the highest log likelihood on the Buffalo Roads validation set. Using

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the training set to finetune the weights in this manner improved the breakeven point

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the NN Mass model to 0.8785. While this number is comparable to the breakeven

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: point of the NN Mass model on the Massachusetts test set it does not mean that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the model works equally well on Buffalo data. In fact, we find that the Buffalo test

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: set appears to be easier than the Massachusetts test set, explaining the comparable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: performance. Nevertheless, these results show that a model trained under one set of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conditions can be adapted to a new dataset using a small amount of labeled training

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: data.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The last model we evaluated on the Buffalo dataset is a post-processing neural

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: network trained on Massachusetts. We applied it to the outputs of the finetuned NN

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Mass model and achieved a breakeven point of 0.8918 on the Buffalo test set. This

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shows that post-processing networks do not necessarily have to be retrained for each

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: new dataset as long as the target object class is the same. Figures 6.3(c) and 6.3(d)

layout_dets.text: Chapter 7

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Conclusions and Future Work

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: This thesis presented a complete framework for learning to label aerial imagery, ad-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vancing the state of the art in both the difficulty of the tasks considered and the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: quality of the predictions. Our framework addressed what we see as the three central

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: issues in learning from aerial imagery – learning of discriminative features, learning

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from noisy data, and doing structured prediction.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In Chapter 3, we showed that neural networks trained on large amounts of la-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: beled images using modern GPUs produced good performance on challenging real

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: world road and building detection datasets. We also showed that deep neural net-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: works produced much more accurate predictions than shallow networks. In particular,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: we found that deep convolutional neural networks with small amounts of maximum

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pooling were particularly effective on aerial image labeling tasks.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Our introduction of noise models for dealing with omission and registration noise

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in Chapter 4 is, to the best of our knowledge, the first attempt to address the problem

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of noisy labels in aerial imagery. It is also, along with the work of Jain [Jain et al.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2010] the first work to directly address the issue of noise in pixel labeling tasks. While

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: our ABN and TABN noise models introduce some level of robustness to two types of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: label noise, we also looked at how noise in the training data affects a system trained on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: this data. By using synthetic omission noise, we found that, somewhat surprisingly,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a neural network trained on a road detection dataset with as much as 40% of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: road labels deleted still performed quite well. Hence, label noise has a negative but

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relatively small effect on neural networks.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Chapter 5 showed that the quality of the predictions can be further improved

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: using two complementary ways of incorporating structure into the predictions of our

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 7. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: system. Post-processing neural networks learn to improve the predictions of a base

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predictor using our patch-framework from Chapter 3. By reusing the existing frame-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: work, post-processing neural networks are able to handle massive datasets using our

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: GPU-based implementation and are capable of learning complex features of the in-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: put predictions. We also showed that adding direct, image-dependent dependencies

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between the outputs of a neural network, turning it into a CRF, improves the predic-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tions by encouraging smoothness between neighbouring labels, a property of the data

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that is not easily learned by post-processing neural networks. While training such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: models can be troublesome, we showed that most of the benefit can be obtained by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: training the neural network separately before using its weights to initialize a CRF.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Finally, we introduced the first large-scale publicly available datasets for both road

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and building detection along with benchmarks that others can compare to. In both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: datasets, the regions used for testing are both much larger and more varied than any

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aerial image labeling dataset, both public or private, that we are aware of. We believe

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that the availability of large and realistic datasets for aerial image labeling has the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: potential to significantly advance the area. In particular, we hope that these datasets

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: will stimulate interest among computer vision and machine learning researchers.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: While there are many possible directions for improving our system, it is important

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to consider which ones will lead to the biggest gain in the quality of predictions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Despite the significant gains obtained by incorporating structured prediction into our

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: system in Chapter 5, it is clear that neural network design choices such as using

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: several layers instead of one and convolutions instead of locally connected units lead

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to the biggest gains in our thesis. For this reason we believe that putting more effort

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: into finding a good neural network architecture is likely to lead to further significant

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: gains. As we mentioned earlier, one way of improving the architecture is by doing a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: better hyper-parameter search using Bayesian optimization techniques [Snoek et al.,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2012]. The recently introduced stochastic pooling [Zeiler and Fergus, 2013] has been

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shown to work much better than the max pooling operation we use and should be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: explored within our system.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In addition to finding a good neural network architecture, it is also important

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to have a good procedure for fitting it to the data. While we have shown that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stochastic gradient descent on the negative log likelihood works well, we believe that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: exploring better loss functions is likely to lead to big improvements in the predictions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: For example, the area under the precision-recall curve is a better measure of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 7. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: quality of the predictions for road and building detection than log likelihood, hence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: directly maximizing the area under the curve is almost certainly a better approach.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Furthermore, due to the fact that even our largest models do not seem to suffer from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: serious overfitting problems, we believe that exploring better optimization methods

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is a promising direction.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Beyond improving the architecture and training procedure of the neural network,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: improving the structured prediction aspect of the model is also likely to lead to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: significant improvements. The fully connected CRF model recently introduced by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Krähenbühl and Koltun [2011] has significantly improved the state-of-the-art in image

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: labeling and is likely to work well on aerial imagery. One interesting question relating

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to these types of models is whether their performance could be improved by jointly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: training all parameters using the model likelihood. We had limited success with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: finetuning the unary potentials of our CRFs using the CRF likelihood, which could

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: simply be the result of using a poor approximate learning procedure. Still, we believe

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that an end-to-end training procedure is preferable to one in which components are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: learned separately.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Another important aspect of the overall system design is what data it is trained

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on, which is equivalent to an underlying assumption about what type of data the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: system is expected to work on. We have focused on improving performance on several

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: large and realistic aerial image labeling datasets, the most diverse of which covered

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: different parts of the state of Massachusetts. Our success on such datasets suggests

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that given enough aerial imagery of a geographic area of limited size it is possible

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to learn a good road or building detector for this area. Ultimately, the goal of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: field is probably to build a system that works well for imagery taken from any part

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the world under any reasonable conditions. While we showed some success with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: training on one region while testing on another one and with adapting an existing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: system to a new region using a small amount of labeled data, building a single good

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: detector probably requires even more varied datasets that cover all distinct regions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the world. Unfortunately, at this point, freely available high resolution imagery is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generally limited to parts of Europe and North America.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Furthermore, being able to label pixels of an aerial image with semantic classes is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not the ultimate goal of aerial image interpretation but merely a useful abstraction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the underlying problems. To make our system truly useful it must be incorporated

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: into a Geographic Information System (GIS). Two possible use cases for a pixel label-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CHAPTER 7. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ing system in a GIS environment are map updating and automatic object extraction.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In the case of map updating, an existing, possibly outdated map needs to be updated

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: based on recent aerial imagery. While maps are usually stored in vector form and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: our system produces raster images as its predictions, comparing a vector map and a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: raster predicted map should be relatively straightforward. By looking for parts of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predicted map that significantly disagree with the reference vector map, our system

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: could be used to automatically find regions that need updating. We believe that the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: quality of the predictions of our system on the Massachusetts Roads data is already

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sufficient to make it useful in an updating setting.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Finally, we believe that our system could also be used to facilitate automatic ex-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: traction of objects from aerial imagery. In the case of roads, this requires extracting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vector representations of road centerlines from predicted raster maps. We have ex-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perimented with the automatic line extraction algorithm of Steger [1998] and found

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that it works well when applied to predicted road maps produced by our system. It is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: interesting that this algorithm was originally applied to extracting roads directly from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aerial imagery, but it works substantially better when applied to the output of our

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: system. This suggests that previous work on finding roads by applying active contour

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: models directly to aerial images can be revisited using our predicted maps as input.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The combination of strong topological constraints enforced by such models with a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: data association potential produced by our system could be especially powerful. In

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the case of buildings, we can already extract their locations by finding the centres

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of mass of connected components of predicted building pixels. Extracting complete

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: building footprints would likely require training on even higher resolution input data,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: but could probably be done using existing polygon extraction algorithms. Again, we

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: see the possibility of using the outputs of our system as a powerful data association

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: term in existing building detection methods that use strong topological constraints.
